title: Beit din
subtitle: Court, mikveh, brit, and a new life
intro: How the beit din for giyur is structured, how the path to giyur differs among the movements, what questions are asked at the interview, how the mikveh and brit milah proceed, and what it means to live as a Jew after giyur.

overview.why: The beit din is the place where the decision to become a Jew becomes a reality: before a court of three, a person accepts the mitzvot, undergoes brit milah (for men), and immerses in the mikveh. By understanding how and why giyur is structured, you see that entering the people of Israel is not a formality, but a covenant that determines your entire subsequent life.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din, three things are checked: the sincerity of your motivation, your understanding of what you are committing to, and the extent to which you already live a Jewish life at the level your congregation expects. Be ready to answer in your own words about your actual practice: Shabbat, kashrut, faith, family, and community — and also work out in advance how the mikveh, brit milah, and naming will proceed.
goals: After this section you will be able to explain what the beit din for giyur is and the three components of giyur
After this section you will be able to compare the path to giyur in the Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform movements
After this section you will be able to answer typical interview questions calmly and honestly
After this section you will be able to prepare for tevilah, brit milah, or hatafat dam brit and to choose a Jewish name
After this section you will be able to describe the status of the ger and how to continue a Jewish life after giyur

lessons.title: What is the beit din for giyur
keyIdeas: Giyur is acceptance into the Jewish people; one who has undergone it is called a ger or giyoret and becomes a full member of the people.
Giyur is performed before three judges because it is a “judicial” act (Yevamot 46b).
The components of giyur: kabbalat mitzvot, brit milah for men (or hatafat dam brit), and tevilah in the mikveh.

Kabbalat mitzvot is the heart of giyur: without it, the rituals do not make a person a Jew. According to the Talmud, one accepts the entire system of mitzvot; the movements understand the obligation differently.
Judaism does not require giyur of non-Jews: a righteous person of the nations of the world has a share in the world to come, and giyur is a voluntary acceptance of obligations.

blocks.text: The word **giyur** (גִּיּוּר) means “acceptance into the Jewish people.” A person who has undergone giyur is called a **ger** (man) or **giyoret** (woman). In the Tanakh the word “ger” originally meant “sojourner,” “one living among strangers,” but in the language of the Sages it came to denote one who has entered the people of Israel and accepted its Torah. Giyur is not the signing of a paper and not an exam in the usual sense. It is entry into the covenant (*brit*) that the Almighty made with the people of Israel at Mount Sinai. That is why the decision about giyur is made not by one person and not by the candidate himself, but by the **beit din** — the Jewish court.

blocks.he: גֵּר, גִּיּוֹרֶת
blocks.text: A person who has accepted Judaism through giyur. In traditional texts also “ger tzedek,” “righteous ger,” as distinct from “ger toshav” — a non-Jew living in the Land of Israel and observing the seven Noahide laws.
Why a court of three specifically

The Talmud (Yevamot 46b) says: “A ger requires three,” that is, giyur is performed before three judges. The Sages derive this from a verse of the Torah in which the ger is referred to by the word **mishpat** — “law,” “judgment”: every judicial matter in Jewish law is considered by a panel of no fewer than three. Therefore the entry of the ger into the people is also a “judicial” act, which must be performed publicly, before witnesses-judges, and not in secret and not by the person's wish alone.

blocks.he: תּוֹרָה אַחַת וּמִשְׁפָּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם וְלַגֵּר הַגָּר אִתְּכֶם
blocks.translit: Torah achat u-mishpat echad yihyeh lachem ve-la-ger ha-gar itchem
blocks.ru: One Torah and one law shall be for you and for the stranger who dwells among you

blocks.text: This same verse also expresses the main idea: after giyur, **the same Torah and the same law** apply to the ger as to a Jew by birth. The ger is not a “second-class Jew” but a full member of the people. That is precisely why the decision itself is taken so seriously: according to halacha there is no way back “out of Judaism.”
The three components of giyur

Rambam in the Mishneh Torah (Laws of Forbidden Relations, *Issurei Biah*, ch. 13) explains that the entire people of Israel entered the covenant through three things: **circumcision** (brit milah), **immersion** (tevilah), and **a sacrifice** (korban). This was so at the Exodus from Egypt and at Mount Sinai, and so, writes Rambam, in every generation: a non-Jew wishing to enter the covenant must undergo circumcision (if a man), immersion, and bring a sacrifice. A woman undergoes immersion and brings a sacrifice. Today, when there is no Temple, the sacrifice is not brought, and giyur is accomplished by circumcision and immersion.

items: **Kabbalat mitzvot** — taking upon oneself the mitzvot of the Torah before the beit din. It is the heart of giyur: without a sincere acceptance of the mitzvot, neither circumcision nor the mikveh makes a person a Jew.
**Brit milah** — for men; if a man is already circumcised, a symbolic *hatafat dam brit* is performed (a drop of the blood of the covenant).
**Tevilah** — complete immersion in the mikveh in the presence of the beit din (in detail — in lesson 4).

blocks.he: קַבָּלַת מִצְוֹת
blocks.text: “Acceptance of the mitzvot” — the candidate's declaration before the beit din that he takes upon himself the obligations of a Jew according to the Torah.

How important kabbalat mitzvot is can be seen from the Talmud (Bechorot 30b): a non-Jew who comes to accept the entire Torah except for one single mitzvah is not accepted. A person is not required to know everything — no one knows everything — but he must be ready to accept the entire system of mitzvot as binding upon himself, and not to choose only what he likes.

In Orthodox halacha (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268) the judges of the beit din must be observant Jews eligible to serve as witnesses; they must not be relatives of one another or of the candidate. Kabbalat mitzvot and tevilah must take place before three judges, and the giyur itself is performed by day and, as a rule, not on Shabbat or a festival, because it is an act of the court.
The order of acceptance according to the Talmud
The most detailed description of how a ger is accepted is in the tractate Yevamot (47a–b). The Sages teach: when in our time a person comes who wishes to become a Jew, they say to him:

blocks.he: מָה רָאִיתָ שֶׁבָּאתָ לְהִתְגַּיֵּר? אִי אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה דְּווּיִים, דְּחוּפִים, סְחוּפִים וּמְטֹרָפִין, וְיִסּוּרִין בָּאִין עֲלֵיהֶן?
blocks.translit: Mah ra'ita she-bata lehitgayer? Iy ata yode'a she-Yisrael ba-zman ha-ze duvim, dechufim, sechufim u-metorafin, ve-yissurin ba'in aleihem?
blocks.ru: What have you seen that you have come to accept Judaism? Do you not know that Israel in this time is afflicted, driven, humiliated, and harassed, and that troubles come upon it?

blocks.text: If the person answers, “I know — and I am not worthy (to be with them),” he is accepted at once. Then they inform him of some of the lighter and some of the weightier mitzvot, telling him of the punishment for violating the mitzvot and the reward for keeping them. Here the Talmud stresses: **“they do not burden him excessively and do not press him too hard.”** The task is not to frighten the person but to give him an honest picture. If he accepts — circumcision is performed, and after it has healed — immersion, and at the immersion two Sages again inform him of some of the mitzvot.

Rambam (Issurei Biah 14:1–2) repeats this order and adds the essential point: the candidate is told **the foundations of faith** — the unity of the Almighty and the prohibition of idolatry — and this is explained to him in detail. And in 13:14 he explains why the examination is needed: the beit din finds out whether the person is coming for money, social position, out of fear, or for the sake of marriage. If the reason is external, the giyur is postponed; if it is sincere, he is accepted.
Be among the disciples of Aaron: love peace and pursue peace, love people and bring them closer to the Torah.
Push away with the left hand, draw near with the right

Many have heard that rabbis “refuse the candidate three times.” There is no strict law about three refusals; it is a custom of some communities, grown out of the Talmud's idea of testing sincerity. The Talmud also has the other side: the famous story of Hillel (Shabbat 31a), who patiently accepted several non-Jews rejected by the stricter Shammai, and said to one of them: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary; go and learn.” The tradition seeks balance: not to accept frivolously, but not to push away the sincere.
If you are told “wait,” “keep studying,” or even “no” — this is usually not a verdict but part of the examination. Calmly ask what exactly you should deepen, and continue on your way.
Is giyur obligatory?

It is important to understand: Judaism does not require non-Jews to become Jews. A righteous person of the nations of the world who observes the seven Noahide laws has, according to Jewish tradition, a share in the world to come. Therefore giyur is not “salvation” but a **voluntary acceptance of additional obligations**. On the other hand, after giyur the obligations become full: the ger is obligated to observe the mitzvot just like any Jew, and his giyur is not annulled even if he later ceases to observe. The Talmud (Yevamot 47b) says of such a person: he is a Jew who has strayed, but still a Jew.

differs.text: In Reform (progressive) Judaism, kabbalat mitzvot is understood as the acceptance of the Jewish faith, destiny, and way of life of the congregation, and a commitment to continue learning and to observe the mitzvot consciously; individual mitzvot the person chooses and deepens himself, rather than accepting the whole halacha as binding law. The beit din usually consists of a rabbi (or rabbis) and representatives of the congregation.

In Conservative Judaism (Masorti), halacha is recognized as binding, but as interpreted by the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Rabbinical Assembly; the beit din consists of three rabbis or knowledgeable observant Jews, and in a number of congregations women also serve on it.

blocks.text: In all movements of Judaism, giyur is performed before a beit din, and in all of them the candidate declares that he binds his destiny to the people of Israel and its Torah. What differs is **what exactly** is accepted as binding and who may be a judge.

lessons.title: The path to giyur in the different movements
keyIdeas: All movements agree that giyur requires study, life in a community, and a beit din, but they understand differently what it means to be obligated by the mitzvot.
An Orthodox beit din expects the candidate to already be living as an observant Jew; the process usually takes from one to three years.
Masorti giyur includes study, usually about a year, participation in a community, a beit din of three, obligatory tevilah, and for men brit milah or hatafat dam brit.
Progressive giyur is built on knowledge, sincerity, and life in a community. Brit milah is obligatory for men in ROOPI and in Israel; in North American Reform it formally is not.
Civil recognition under the Law of Return differs from religious recognition; an Orthodox giyur is recognized by all movements.

blocks.text: In today's world, giyur is conducted by the different movements of Judaism: Orthodox, Conservative (in Israel and Europe it is called **Masorti**), and Reform (Progressive). All of them agree that giyur is a serious, carefully considered decision requiring study, life in a community, and a beit din. But they understand differently **what it means to be obligated by the mitzvot**, and therefore they structure the path differently. Here we will try to describe each path as the movements themselves describe it — without ratings of “better” or “worse”. The choice of path is your personal question, which is worth discussing with the rabbi of your community.
Common steps for everyone

items: A meeting with the community rabbi and a conversation about motivation.
Study: the foundations of faith, the Torah, prayer, Shabbat, kashrut, the holidays, history, Hebrew.
Life in the community: prayers, Shabbatot, holidays, getting to know people.
Gradual observance of the mitzvot in your own life.
An interview before the beit din.
The giyur rituals: for men — brit milah or hatafat dam brit; for everyone — tevilah in a mikveh (with caveats for some Reform communities).
Receiving a Jewish name and a document (certificate) of giyur.

blocks.text: Orthodox giyur

Orthodox Judaism proceeds from the premise that the Torah — the Written and the Oral — was given by the Almighty and that halacha is fully binding. Therefore an Orthodox beit din expects that by the time of giyur the candidate **is already living as an observant Jew**: observes Shabbat and the holidays, keeps a kosher home, prays, observes the laws of modesty and (for married people) the laws of family purity. An important requirement is to live near an Orthodox community, within walking distance of a synagogue, since driving is not permitted on Shabbat.

The timeline depends on the person and the beit din, but the path usually takes **from one to three years**. There is almost always a mentor rabbi who guides the candidate and then recommends him to the court. Special attention is paid to motivation: if a person is coming in order to marry a Jew, the beit din checks whether he or she has a personal aspiration toward the Torah (Rambam, Issurei Biah 13:14). If the candidate lives with a Jewish partner, they are usually required to stop living together before the giyur.

There are also differences within the Orthodox world. In Israel, state giyur is conducted by special courts attached to the Chief Rabbinate, and preparatory programs exist (for example, “Nativ”). Recognition of giyur can vary: the Chief Rabbinate of Israel does not recognize all Orthodox batei din abroad, only those it has approved. If it matters to you to be able to marry through the Rabbinate, find out the status of the beit din you choose in advance.

Orthodox giyur is recognized by all movements of Judaism. Therefore some people choose it precisely, even if they themselves will later live in a non-Orthodox community. This is a question of personal choice, not of obligation.
Conservative (Masorti) giyur

Conservative Judaism considers halacha binding but evolving: it is interpreted by the rabbis of the movement (in the USA — the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Rabbinical Assembly). Masorti giyur includes study (usually about a year, sometimes longer), participation in the life of the community, a beit din of three, obligatory tevilah, and for men — brit milah or hatafat dam brit. The candidate takes upon himself or herself the observance of Shabbat, kashrut, and the other mitzvot **as understood in Conservative halacha** — for example, many Conservative communities allow driving to synagogue by car on Shabbat, and men and women pray together.

Conservative giyur is recognized by Conservative and Reform communities, and for purposes of the Law of Return — by the State of Israel; Orthodox batei din and the Israeli Rabbinate do not recognize it.
Reform (Progressive) giyur

Reform Judaism sees the Torah as a path inspired by the Almighty but changing over time; each Jew personally and consciously decides which mitzvot to observe and how, relying on knowledge and on the life of the community. Therefore progressive giyur is built not on checking full observance, but on **knowledge, sincerity, and involvement in the community**.

In Russia and the CIS countries, progressive giyur is conducted by ROOPI (the Union of Religious Organizations of Progressive Judaism), which belongs to the World Union for Progressive Judaism (WUPJ). According to the description of the giyur school of the St. Petersburg community “Shaarei Shalom,” the path includes:

items: **a motivation letter** — an account of yourself and of why you are drawn to Judaism;
**no less than a year of study** in a giyur school;
**regular participation in the life of the community** — services, holidays, community events;
a beit din and immersion in a mikveh;
for men, **brit milah is obligatory**.

blocks.text: Reform giyur is recognized by Reform and many Conservative communities, and for purposes of the Law of Return — by the State of Israel. Orthodox batei din and the Rabbinate do not recognize it. In Israel, progressive giyur is conducted by the Israel Movement for Progressive Judaism (IMPJ).

differs.text: In the Reform movement of North America, brit milah and tevilah have not been formally required since the late 19th century, and many rabbis merely recommend them; in ROOPI communities and in Israel they are part of the giyur procedure.

blocks.text: Please note: Reform rules differ from country to country, so always rely on the requirements of the specific community and its rabbi.

The brief sketch in this lesson gives a map. The Reform giyur is examined in detail — with the same thoroughness as the account of the Orthodox path — in the lesson “Reform Giyur: Study, Community, and Beit Din”.
The Israeli Law of Return — in general terms

The Law of Return (1950) gives every Jew the right to repatriate to Israel. The 1970 amendment determined that for the purposes of the law a Jew is someone born to a Jewish mother or someone who has undergone giyur and does not profess another religion; the right to repatriation is also granted to the children and grandchildren of Jews and to their spouses. A giyur completed abroad in a recognized Jewish community of any of the major movements is, according to the decisions of the Supreme Court of Israel, usually recognized for repatriation. As a rule, they check that the giyur was completed in an active community after a real period of study, and that the ger continues to participate in its life. The exact criteria change and should be verified with the Jewish Agency (Sochnut) and with a rabbi.

It is important to distinguish **civil recognition** (the right to repatriation) from **religious recognition** (for example, for marrying through the Chief Rabbinate of Israel). The latter in Israel today applies only to an Orthodox giyur approved by the Rabbinate.

Before starting the path, ask yourself honestly: in which community do I want to live? How do I want to raise my children? Do I need a marriage through the Rabbinate? The answers will help you choose a movement, and a rabbi will help you find the way to it.

cards.back: That the giyur was completed in an active community after a real period of study, and that the ger continues to participate in its life; the criteria change — check with Sochnut.

lessons.title: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11
keyIdeas: The judges want to make sure that the decision is sincere, that you understand the obligations, and that you are already living a Jewish life to the extent expected by your community.
The main question is “What did you see?” — a good answer is personal and specific, not general or external.
Be prepared to say clearly that you believe in the One G-d and no longer belong to another religion.
About Shabbat, kashrut, family, and community, speak about what you actually do; honesty matters more than an ideal picture.
Ruth’s words “Your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d” are, in essence, the best short answer to the beit din — if you show how they sound in your own life.

blocks.text: The interview at the beit din makes almost every candidate nervous. It is useful to understand its purpose from the very start: the judges are not trying to “fail” you. They want to be sure of three things — that your decision is **sincere**, that you **understand** what you are committing to, and that you are **already living** a Jewish life to the extent expected by your community. Knowledge matters, but honesty matters even more. The judges are experienced people; they will quickly recognize a memorized “correct” answer, while an uncertain but honest “I am still working on this” earns respect.

The sample answers in this lesson and in the exam questions are only a guide, not a script. Answer in your own words and about your own real life. If you do not know something or do not yet observe something — say so.
1. Motivation: “Why do you want to become a Jew?”

This is the most ancient question of giyur — “What did you see?” (Yevamot 47a). A good answer is personal and specific: what brought you to Judaism, what you have discovered in the Torah, in Shabbat, in the community, why you feel that this is your people. A bad answer is a general one (“I like the culture”) or an external one (“it makes marriage easier,” “I want to move to Israel”). If your story includes a Jewish partner or Jewish ancestors, do not hide it: say honestly how it influenced you and why this has now become **your own** choice.

Almost always they also ask what the Talmud asked: **do you know that the Jewish people have suffered and still suffer?** Are you prepared to share the fate of the people, including antisemitism? Here the honest answer is to say that you understand this and consciously choose to be with this people, like Ruth, who said to Naomi: “Your people shall be my people.”
2. “Why not remain a righteous person of the nations of the world?”

An experienced beit din often asks: if a non-Jew can be righteous by observing the seven Noahide laws (Rambam, Laws of Kings 8:11), why do you need to take upon yourself 613 mitzvot? This question checks whether you understand that giyur is not a path to “salvation” but the acceptance of **obligations**. You can answer like this: “I know that I could be righteous even so. But I want not only to be a good person — I want to belong to the covenant of Israel, to live by the Torah and to pass it on to my children.”
3. Faith

You will be asked what you believe: about the Almighty, about the Torah, about prayer. Rambam (Issurei Biah 14:2) writes directly that the candidate is explained in detail **the unity of the Almighty and the prohibition of idolatry**. Therefore be prepared to say clearly that you believe in the One G-d, that you no longer belong to another religion, and that you do not take part in its rituals. Those who grew up in another faith are often asked about their attitude toward it: the answer must be unambiguous — you believe only in the One G-d, no human being is G-d for you, Mashiach has not yet come, and you no longer connect your faith with your former teachings.

In an Orthodox beit din the questions about faith go deeper: do you believe that the whole Torah, including the Oral Torah, was given by the Almighty to Moshe at Sinai; that He rewards and punishes; that Mashiach will come. This relies on Rambam’s 13 principles of faith. Doubts are a normal part of the life of a person of faith, but acceptance of these fundamentals as truth is obligatory here.

Rambam requires that the unity of the Almighty be explained to the candidate in detail (Issurei Biah 14:2), so be prepared to talk about your faith in G-d; they also often ask about Mashiach. Answer clearly and calmly: G-d is one and indivisible, He has no body or form, and He does not become a human being (Devarim 6:4; Bamidbar 23:19). Mashiach is a human being, a king from the house of David; he has not yet come, and his coming will be the first and only one. In detail — in the “Foundations” section, the lessons “One and Indivisible” and “Mashiach”.

About faith the judges want to hear something simple and clear. G-d is one, without “persons” and without a body; one prays only to Him; the Torah is eternal; Mashiach is a human being from the house of David, and he has not yet come. If you grew up in another faith, calmly say that you have left it behind and do not take part in its services. There is no need to argue with other people’s teachers at the hearing; what matters is what you yourself believe now.
4. Shabbat and kashrut

These are questions about practice, and they are asked very concretely: “Tell us how your Shabbat goes — from lighting the candles to havdalah.” “What do you do if work calls you on Shabbat?” “How is your kitchen organized?” “What do you do when you eat out?” Speak about what you actually do. A description of a real Friday evening — the candles, kiddush, challah, prayer in the synagogue, the phone switched off — convinces more than a list of the 39 forbidden labors.

In an Orthodox beit din they expect full observance: separate dishes for meat and dairy, only products with reliable kashrut, waiting between meat and dairy according to your community’s custom, observance of all the Shabbat prohibitions. They may ask details: whether it is permitted to heat food on Shabbat, what muktzeh is, how eggs are checked for blood.

differs.text: In a Reform beit din you are asked about Shabbat and kashrut in terms of how you meaningfully mark Shabbat and what decisions about food you have made for your home; full halachic observance is not a condition of giyur.

blocks.text: If you are still learning and something is not working out yet — say so directly and explain how you are progressing. An honest “I still sometimes mix up the dishes, but I have already set aside separate sets” is a good answer.
5. Family

The beit din is interested in your loved ones: how your parents reacted to the decision, whether you have a spouse or partner, how you will raise your children. The judges want to see that you have thought through the difficulties: holidays with non-Jewish relatives, food in your parents’ home, questions about children. A good answer shows both **respect for parents** and firmness of decision. If you have children, be prepared to discuss their status: in Orthodox and Conservative halacha, children born before the mother’s giyur do not automatically become Jews, and they need a separate giyur.
6. Community

“Which synagogue do you attend? Who is your rabbi? How do you help the community?” Judaism is a religion of community: many prayers are recited only with a minyan, and the holidays are celebrated together. Name the people and events in which you take part. Tell them how you see your place in the community after the giyur.

A community is a place where you learn and celebrate, and it is chosen carefully. Ask which movement it belongs to and who its rabbi is. A congregation that looks Jewish but teaches about G-d in several persons or about a Mashiach who has already come is not a Jewish community, even if there is a kippah and holidays there. When in doubt, it is better to ask your own beit din than to decide alone.
7. Knowledge

Usually they check the basics: the Shema and its meaning, the blessings over food, the order of the holidays, the meaning of Yom Kippur and Pesach, the basic laws of Shabbat and kashrut, why we eat matzah, who the forefathers and foremothers are. Sometimes they ask you to read a short prayer in Hebrew. Knowledge shows that you studied seriously, but do not worry about one forgotten fact.

items: Answer briefly and to the point; if a question is unclear — ask again.
Do not exaggerate your practice: it is easy to check, and a lie destroys trust.
Speak about yourself: “I do,” “I feel,” not “Jews must.”
Do not be afraid of a pause — it is normal to think before answering.
Dress modestly and neatly; to an Orthodox beit din men come in a kippah, women — in a skirt with covered shoulders (married women — with the head covered).

blocks.he: עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי
blocks.ru: Your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d

blocks.text: These words of Ruth are, in essence, the best short answer to all the beit din’s questions: belonging to the people and faith in the G-d of Israel together. Your task is to show how they sound in your own life.

cards.front: What three things does the beit din want to see?
cards.back: The sincerity of the decision, understanding of the obligations, and the candidate’s real Jewish life.

cards.front: What matters more at the interview — knowledge or honesty?
cards.back: Honesty. Knowledge is needed, but memorized “correct” answers and exaggerations do harm.

cards.front: What should the answer about motivation be like?
cards.back: Personal and specific: what brought you to Judaism and why this is your own choice.

cards.front: Is it worth hiding that you have a Jewish partner?
cards.back: No. Answer honestly and explain why giyur became your own decision.

cards.front: Why does the beit din ask about the suffering of the Jews?
cards.back: This is the question of Yevamot 47a: are you ready to share the fate of the people, including antisemitism.

cards.front: What does the question “why not remain a righteous person of the nations of the world?” test?
cards.back: Whether you understand that giyur is the acceptance of obligations, not the only path to righteousness.

cards.front: Where does Rambam write that the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the World to Come?
cards.back: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11.

cards.front: Which fundamentals of faith does the beit din explain to the candidate according to Rambam (14:2)?
cards.back: The unity of the Almighty and the prohibition of idolatry.

cards.front: How should you answer the question about your former faith (if you grew up in another religion)?
cards.back: Unambiguously: I believe only in the One G-d; no human being is G-d; Mashiach has not yet come; I do not take part in the former rituals.

cards.front: What additional matters of faith does an Orthodox beit din ask about?
cards.back: About the divinity of the entire Torah, including the Oral Torah, about reward and punishment, about Mashiach (the 13 principles).

cards.front: What is the best way to talk about Shabbat?
cards.back: Describe a real Shabbat: candles, kiddush, prayer, rest, havdalah — rather than reciting lists.

cards.front: Do a Jew's children automatically become Jewish after their mother's giyur (Orth./Cons.)?
cards.back: No, if they were born before her giyur — they need a separate giyur.

cards.front: Why does the beit din ask about the community?
cards.back: Judaism is a religion of community: minyan, festivals, mutual help.

cards.front: How should you dress for an Orthodox beit din?
cards.back: Modestly: men in a kippah; women in a skirt, with shoulders covered, married women with a covered head.

cards.front: “Amech ami ve-Elohayich Elohai” — what is this and where is it from?
cards.back: “Your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d” — the words of Ruth (Rut 1:16).

cards.front: What does the knowledge section of the questions usually test?
cards.back: The Shema and its meaning, blessings over food, the order of the festivals, the meaning of Yom Kippur and Pesach, why we eat matzah, the forefathers and foremothers.

cards.front: What should you do if you don't understand a judge's question?
cards.back: Calmly ask again — that is normal and better than answering the wrong question.

cards.front: Is it okay to pause before answering the judge?
cards.back: Yes, taking a moment to think before answering is normal; don't be afraid of a pause.

cards.front: What details of practice might you be asked about in an Orthodox beit din?
cards.back: Heating food on Shabbat, what muktzeh is, checking eggs for blood spots; also separate dishes, kashrut of products, and waiting between meat and dairy.

cards.front: Why does the beit din ask how your parents reacted to your decision?
cards.back: The judges want to see that you have thought through the difficulties and maintain respect for your parents while remaining firm in your decision.

cards.front: What mistake do people make when answering “Jews must…”?
cards.back: They speak about others instead of themselves; it is more convincing to say “I do,” “I feel.”

cards.front: What do Ruth's words mean as a short answer to the beit din?
cards.back: Belonging to the people of Israel and faith in the G-d of Israel together; the candidate's task is to show how they sound in his or her life.

cards.front: How to briefly answer the beit din: has Mashiach already come?
cards.back: No. In Judaism Mashiach has not yet come; we await him, and his coming will be the first and only one. There is no “second coming” in Judaism.

cards.front: How to briefly answer the beit din about the unity of G-d?
cards.back: G-d is one and indivisible: without a body or form, not “three faces” and not a human being (Devarim 6:4; Bamidbar 23:19). I pray only to Him.

lessons.title: Mikveh: the Immersion of the Ger
keyIdeas: Tevilah completes the giyur: at the moment of coming out of the water, the ger or giyoret becomes a Jew.
A kosher mikveh is a pool of natural water that flowed in by itself, not drawn into vessels; its volume is no less than 40 seah.
There must be no chatzitzah between the body and the water, so before immersion one washes thoroughly and removes everything unnecessary.
The blessing “al ha-tevilah” is said after immersion: only after emerging from the water as a Jew can the ger say “who has commanded us.”
Tevilah takes place by day before three judges, with careful attention to modesty, especially for women.

blocks.text: Immersion in the mikveh — **tevilah** — completes the giyur. For a woman it is the only bodily rite of giyur; for a man it is the second, after brit milah. At the moment the ger or giyoret emerges from the water, he or she becomes a Jew. Therefore people prepare for tevilah seriously, and the rite itself proceeds calmly, solemnly, and with great attention to modesty.

blocks.he: מִקְוֶה
blocks.text: “A gathering (of waters)” — a pool of natural water, not drawn into vessels, with a volume of no less than 40 seah; used for purification and for giyur.

blocks.he: אַךְ מַעְיָן וּבוֹר מִקְוֵה מַיִם יִהְיֶה טָהוֹר
blocks.translit: Ach ma'ayan u-vor mikveh mayim yihyeh tahor
blocks.ru: But a spring or a cistern, a gathering of waters, shall be pure

blocks.text: What is a mikveh

From this verse the Sages derive the laws of the mikveh. A kosher mikveh is not just a pool. Its water must be **natural**: rain, spring, or melted water, and it must enter the mikveh by itself, not be brought in buckets or other vessels. The minimum volume is **40 seah** (by various calculations, several hundred liters), enough for an adult to immerse completely. Modern mikvaot usually have a reservoir of rainwater connected to the pool in a special way, while the water in the pool itself may be heated and purified. The sea, as well as a natural lake or river, can also serve as a mikveh according to halacha, but with qualifications (for example, regarding rivers fed by rain), so the decision to immerse in a natural body of water is made by a rabbi.

A mikveh is used not only for giyur. Married women immerse in it according to the laws of family purity, many men — before Shabbat and Yom Kippur, and new dishes bought from non-Jews are dipped in a special mikveh for dishes. For giyur, specifically a kosher mikveh for people is required, and tevilah takes place under the supervision of a beit din.

blocks.he: טְבִילָה
blocks.text: Complete immersion of the body in the mikveh's water in a single act, so that the water touches every part of the body and the hair.
Preparation: what is a chatzitzah

The main condition of tevilah is that **nothing** be between the body and the water. Anything that separates the body from the water is called a **chatzitzah** (interposition). If a significant interposition remains on the body — one that matters to the person — the immersion may be invalid. Therefore, thorough preparation is done before tevilah:

blocks.he: חֲצִיצָה
blocks.text: “Interposition” — any substance or object between the body and the water of the mikveh.

items: take a shower or bath, wash the entire body and hair thoroughly;
comb the hair so there are no knots or tangles;
remove all jewelry, rings, earrings, piercings, watches, hairpins, hair ties;
remove contact lenses, removable dentures (if possible), plasters and bandages;
remove cosmetics, nail polish, glue residue, paint, dirt under the nails; many people trim their nails short;
brush your teeth, clean your ears and nose;
use the toilet beforehand.

blocks.text: If you have permanent fillings, crowns, braces, tattoos, stitches, or medical devices — tell the rabbi in advance. Many of these are not considered a chatzitzah, but the question must be settled before the day of giyur, not in the mikveh itself.
How tevilah proceeds

Giyur is performed **by day**, on a weekday: the tevilah of the ger is an act of the beit din, and a court does not sit at night, on Shabbat, or on festivals. At the appointed hour the candidate comes to the mikveh, prepares in a separate room, and an attendant (for women — a female attendant, *ballanit*) checks that no chatzitzah remains. Then the candidate enters the water.

items: The candidate stands in the water. The judges of the beit din briefly remind him of several mitzvot once more, and the candidate confirms that he accepts them.
The candidate immerses completely — so that the water covers the entire body and all the hair at once, and no part of the body remains above the water.
Rising from the water, he or she recites the blessing over immersion.
Then, by custom, one immerses again (and in many communities a third time).

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל הַטְּבִילָה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al ha-tevilah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Lord, our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us concerning immersion

blocks.text: Why is the blessing said **after** immersion, when usually a blessing precedes the mitzvah? Because until immersion the person is not yet a Jew and cannot say “who has commanded us.” Only after emerging from the water as a Jew does the ger give thanks for the mitzvah he has just fulfilled. In many communities the blessing “Shehecheyanu” is then added:

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהֶחֱיָנוּ וְקִיְּמָנוּ וְהִגִּיעָנוּ לַזְּמַן הַזֶּה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, she-hecheyanu ve-kiyemanu ve-higianu la-zman ha-zeh
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Lord, our G-d, King of the universe, who has granted us life, sustained us, and brought us to this time
blocks.ref: Siddur; the custom of many communities at giyur

blocks.text: Witnesses and modesty

Tevilah must take place **before three judges**, with careful attention to modesty. For men, the judges are present at the mikveh during the immersion. For women, the Talmud (Yevamot 47b) describes an order that is still observed today: women help the giyoret enter the water, while the Sages stand outside. In practice, the candidate immerses in the presence of the ballanit; the judges either stand behind a slightly open door and hear the blessing, or enter when she is already in the water, covered by the water and, by the custom of some communities, a loose robe — depending on the custom of the beit din. The judges do not look at her body; their task is to witness the immersion and the acceptance of the mitzvot.

Some details of Orthodox practice: during immersion the body should be relaxed, the arms slightly away from the body, the eyes and lips closed without clenching tightly, so that the water touches all the outer folds. If even a strand of hair remains above the water, the immersion is repeated. The ballanit or attendant watches this and says “kosher” after a valid immersion.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, tevilah is understood as a spiritual symbol of transition; in the communities of ROOPI (the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities) and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it. The immersion is sometimes performed in a natural body of water, with prayers and the candidate's own words added.

blocks.text: After tevilah, many gerim recite “Shema Yisrael” as their first declaration of faith already as Jews. Then the beit din presents the giyur document and, as a rule, announces the new Jewish name.

cards.front: What is tevilah?
cards.back: Complete immersion of the body in the mikveh in a single act — the concluding rite of giyur.

cards.front: What does the word “mikveh” mean?
cards.back: “A gathering (of waters)”: a pool of natural water of no less than 40 seah.

cards.front: From which verse are the laws of the mikveh derived?
cards.back: Vayikra 11:36: “But a spring or a cistern, a gathering of waters, shall be pure.”

cards.front: What water is fit for a mikveh?
cards.back: Natural (rain, spring) water that came by itself, not drawn into vessels.

cards.front: What is the minimum volume of a mikveh?
cards.back: 40 seah — by various calculations, several hundred liters.

cards.front: What is a chatzitzah?
cards.back: An interposition between the body and the water (jewelry, polish, dirt, lenses, etc.).

cards.front: Name 4 steps of preparing for tevilah.
cards.back: Wash and comb; remove jewelry and lenses; remove cosmetics and polish; clean the nails.

cards.front: What should you do about fillings, braces, stitches?
cards.back: Ask the rabbi in advance: much is not considered a chatzitzah, but it must be settled before the giyur.

cards.front: When can the tevilah of a ger not be performed?
cards.back: At night, on Shabbat, and on festivals: it is an act of the beit din, and a court does not sit at those times.

cards.front: What blessing does the ger say at tevilah?
cards.back: “…asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al ha-tevilah” — “…who has commanded us concerning immersion.”

cards.front: Why does the ger say the blessing after immersion?
cards.back: Until immersion he is not yet a Jew and cannot say “who has commanded us.”

cards.front: What blessing do many add after tevilah?
cards.back: “Shehecheyanu” — for the Almighty granting us life to reach this time.

cards.front: How is modesty observed at a woman's tevilah?
cards.back: A female ballanit assists her; the judges stand behind the door or enter when she is covered by the water/robe.

cards.front: What if a strand of hair remains above the water during immersion?
cards.back: The immersion is repeated: the water must cover the whole body and the hair at once.

cards.front: Who must witness the tevilah of a ger?
cards.back: A beit din of three judges.

cards.front: What do many gerim say right after emerging from the mikveh?
cards.back: “Shema Yisrael” — the first declaration of faith already as Jews.

cards.front: When does the beit din present the giyur document and announce the new name?
cards.back: After tevilah.

cards.front: How are modern mikvaot with natural water built?
cards.back: A reservoir of rainwater is connected to the pool in a special way; the water in the pool may be heated and purified.

cards.front: Can the sea, a lake, or a river serve as a mikveh?
cards.back: According to halacha — yes, but with qualifications; the decision to immerse in a natural body of water is made by a rabbi.

cards.front: What is the position of the body during proper immersion (Orthodox practice)?
cards.back: The body is relaxed, the arms slightly away from the body, the eyes and lips closed without tight clenching.

cards.front: How do Reform communities understand tevilah?
cards.back: As a spiritual symbol of transition; in ROOPI and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it.

cards.front: What do the judges do while the candidate stands in the water?
cards.back: They briefly remind him of several mitzvot once more; the candidate confirms that he accepts them.

lessons.title: Brit milah, hatafat dam brit, and the new name
citations: Rambam, Letter to Ovadyah the Ger
keyIdeas: Brit milah is the sign of the Almighty's covenant with Avraham; the adult ger repeats the path of Avraham, who was circumcised at 99.
The ger is circumcised by a mohel for the sake of giyur in the presence of a beit din; tevilah takes place only after healing.
A man who is already circumcised undergoes hatafat dam brit — the drawing of a drop of the blood of the covenant.
The ger receives a Jewish name and is called the son or daughter of Avraham, our forefather.
This name accompanies the ger throughout life and expresses the idea that he or she is a true son or daughter of Avraham and Sarah.

blocks.text: For a man, giyur includes **brit milah** — circumcision. This is not a medical procedure and not a “formality,” but the sign of the covenant that the Almighty made with Avraham and his descendants. For many adult candidates this part is the most frightening of all. Therefore it is useful to calmly work out what this mitzvah is, why it is obligatory, and how everything proceeds in practice.

blocks.he: זֹאת בְּרִיתִי אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׁמְרוּ בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵיכֶם וּבֵין זַרְעֲךָ אַחֲרֶיךָ, הִמּוֹל לָכֶם כָּל זָכָר
blocks.translit: Zot briti asher tishmeru beini u-veineichem u-vein zar'acha acharecha, himol lachem kol zachar
blocks.ru: This is My covenant which you shall keep between Me and you and your offspring after you: every male among you shall be circumcised

blocks.text: Avraham — the First Ger

The Torah relates that Avraham was circumcised at 99 (Bereshit 17:24) — that is, as an adult, by his own decision, having heard the command of the Almighty. Tradition sees Avraham as the “father of gerim”: he left his father's house and his former faith and followed the One G-d. Therefore an adult ger undergoing brit milah literally repeats the path of the forefather. Rambam (Issurei Biah 13:1–4) reminds us that the entire people of Israel also entered the covenant through circumcision and immersion before the Exodus from Egypt and at Sinai; by this model giyur is performed in every generation.

blocks.he: בְּרִית מִילָה
blocks.text: “The covenant of circumcision” — the removal of the foreskin as a sign of Avraham's covenant. A Jewish infant is circumcised on the eighth day; a ger — at his giyur.
How brit milah proceeds for an adult ger

items: The circumcision is performed by a **mohel** — a specialist who knows the laws of milah; for adults this is often a physician-mohel. The procedure is performed in a clinic or a specially equipped room, under local anesthesia.
The milah must be performed **for the sake of giyur** — as part of entering the covenant, in the presence of representatives of the beit din (according to many opinions — three judges).
The mohel recites a special blessing for the circumcision of gerim.
Then time is needed for healing — usually several weeks. Only after that does tevilah take place (Yevamot 47b: “when he has healed — they immerse him”).
Unlike the circumcision of an infant on the eighth day, the milah of a ger does not override the prohibition of Shabbat and is not performed on Shabbat and festivals.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לָמוֹל אֶת הַגֵּרִים וּלְהַטִּיף מֵהֶם דַּם בְּרִית
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu la-mol et ha-gerim u-le-hatif mehem dam brit
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Lord, our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to circumcise the gerim and to draw from them the blood of the covenant

blocks.text: Fear of the operation is normal. Talk to the mohel in advance: ask how the procedure will go, what anesthesia is used, how many days recovery will take, and when you can return to work. Many gerim later remember that day as one of the most significant of their lives.
Hatafat dam brit: if the man is already circumcised

Many men were circumcised in childhood for medical or cultural reasons (for example, Muslims). Such a circumcision was not performed for the sake of the covenant, so instead of a full milah, **hatafat dam brit** is performed — “the drawing of a drop of the blood of the covenant.” The mohel makes a tiny prick at the site of the circumcision so that a drop of blood appears. This takes a minute and is almost painless. The source is a dispute of the Sages in the Talmud (Shabbat 135a) about a ger who came already circumcised; halacha rules that a drop of the blood of the covenant must be drawn from him (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1).

blocks.he: הַטָּפַת דַּם בְּרִית
blocks.text: The symbolic drawing of a drop of blood at the site of the circumcision in an already circumcised man at giyur.

By widespread practice, hatafat dam brit is performed without a blessing, and the laws of the beit din's presence and the subsequent waiting before tevilah are the same as for milah, though healing takes only a few days. Details vary between beit dinim — follow the instructions of yours.

differs.text: In the Reform movement of North America, brit milah for an adult ger is formally not obligatory. However, in ROOPI (the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities), according to the description of the giyur school “Shaarei Shalom,” brit milah for men is obligatory, as it is in Progressive giyur in Israel.

blocks.text: Conservative and Orthodox Judaism require brit milah or hatafat dam brit of every male ger without exception.
The New Jewish Name

At giyur the ger receives a **Jewish name**. Usually the candidate chooses it himself, in consultation with the rabbi. People often choose the names of the forefathers and foremothers, heroes of the Tanakh, or names with personal meaning: men often call themselves Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Ovadyah; women — Ruth, Sarah, Rivka, Naomi. A man receives the name at brit milah or after tevilah, a woman — after tevilah; the name is announced by the beit din and the rabbi.

A Jewish name consists of a personal name and the father's name. Since the parents of a ger are not Jewish, he is called the son or daughter of **Avraham, our forefather**: for example, “David ben Avraham avinu,” “Rut bat Avraham avinu.” In many communities, especially non-Orthodox ones, the foremother's name is added: “ben Avraham ve-Sarah,” “bat Avraham ve-Sarah.”

blocks.he: רוּת בַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ
blocks.ru: Ruth, daughter of Avraham, our forefather
blocks.ref: The custom of naming the ger

blocks.text: The ger will use this name all his life: when he is called up to the Torah, in the ketubah (marriage contract), in prayers for him, and after one hundred and twenty years — on the tombstone. This name expresses the main idea: the ger is not a “stranger,” but a true son or daughter of Avraham and Sarah. In his famous responsum to Ovadyah the ger, Rambam wrote that a ger may say in prayer “our G-d and the G-d of our fathers,” because Avraham is his father.

Choosing a name is a joyful part of the preparation. Think about a person from the Tanakh whose path is close to you, and discuss the choice with the rabbi in advance, so that on the day of giyur you don't have to decide in a rush.

cards.front: What is brit milah?
cards.back: “The covenant of circumcision” — the sign of Avraham's covenant; for a male ger, an obligatory part of giyur.

cards.front: Where in the Torah is the commandment of circumcision?
cards.back: Bereshit 17:9–14 (“every male among you shall be circumcised,” 17:10).

cards.front: At what age did Avraham undergo circumcision?
cards.back: At the age of 99 (Bereshit 17:24).

cards.front: Why is Avraham called “the father of gerim”?
cards.back: He left his father's house and his former faith and went after the One G-d.

cards.front: Who performs the brit milah?
cards.back: A mohel — an expert in the laws of circumcision; for adults it is often a physician-mohel, under local anesthesia.

cards.front: Which comes first for a male ger: milah or tevilah?
cards.back: Milah; tevilah — after the wound has healed (Yevamot 47b).

cards.front: May a ger be circumcised on Shabbat?
cards.back: No: Shabbat is set aside only for the milah of an eight-day-old infant.

cards.front: What is hatafat dam brit?
cards.back: The drawing of a drop of blood at the site of the circumcision of an already circumcised man at giyur.

cards.front: Why is medical circumcision not sufficient for giyur?
cards.back: It was not done for the sake of the covenant; therefore hatafat dam brit is performed (Shabbat 135a; Yoreh De'ah 268:1).

cards.front: What blessing does the mohel recite when circumcising a ger?
cards.back: “…ve-tzivanu la'mol et ha-gerim u-lehatif mehem dam brit” (Yoreh De'ah 268:5).

cards.front: Is brit milah obligatory for men in ROOPI?
cards.back: Yes, according to the description of the giyur school of the “Shaarei Shalom” community; in North American Reform — formally, no.

cards.front: What does a ger’s patronymic sound like in a Jewish name?
cards.back: “Ben/bat Avraham Avinu”; in many communities — “ben/bat Avraham ve-Sarah.”

cards.front: Where is a ger’s Jewish name used?
cards.back: At an aliyah to the Torah, in the ketubah, in prayers for him, on the tombstone.

cards.front: What did Rambam answer Ovadyah the Ger?
cards.back: A ger may say “the G-d of our fathers”: Avraham is his father.

cards.front: Is a blessing recited over hatafat dam brit?
cards.back: By widespread practice — no. Healing takes several days; the presence of the beit din and the pause before the tevilah are as with milah.

cards.front: In whose presence must a ger’s milah be performed?
cards.back: In the presence of representatives of the beit din (by many opinions — three judges), for the sake of the giyur.

cards.front: Are there exceptions from milah in Orthodox and Conservative giyur?
cards.back: No. Both Orthodox and Conservative giyur require brit milah or hatafat dam brit of every man.

cards.front: When does a ger receive a Jewish name?
cards.back: A man — at the brit milah or after the tevilah; a woman — after the tevilah; the beit din and the rabbi announce the name.

cards.front: Which names do gerim often choose?
cards.back: Men — Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Ovadyah; women — Ruth, Sarah, Rivka, Naomi.

cards.front: How and when should one choose a Jewish name?
cards.back: The candidate himself, consulting the rabbi in advance, so as not to decide in a rush on the day of the giyur.

cards.front: What is worth asking the mohel in advance?
cards.back: How the procedure will go, what pain relief is used, how many days recovery takes, and when one can return to work.

lessons.title: After giyur: the life of a ger
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Character Traits (De'ot) 6:4
Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels (Mamrim) 5:11
keyIdeas: “A ger who has accepted Judaism is like a newborn child”: he is a full Jew, obligated in all the mitzvot and possessing all rights.
The Torah repeatedly commands not to wrong a ger and to love him; according to Rambam, loving a ger is two mitzvot.
One may not remind a ger of his past or his origin — this is onaat devarim, verbal oppression.
Giyur does not mean a break with the family: a ger must respect his non-Jewish parents, but does not take part in the rites of another religion.
After giyur it is important to keep learning: to find a teacher and a chevruta, to remain an active member of the community.

blocks.text: Emerging from the mikveh, a ger or giyoret becomes a Jew — fully and forever. This is not the end of the path, but its true beginning. In this lesson we will talk about a ger’s status in Jewish law, how the community should relate to him, how to preserve relations with relatives, and how to keep growing in Torah.
A full Jew

The Talmud (Yevamot 22a) says: **“A ger who has accepted Judaism is like a newborn child.”** His former sins no longer weigh upon him, and he begins a new life among the people of Israel. A ger is obligated to observe all the mitzvot, like any Jew, and has all rights: he is called to the Torah, he counts in the minyan, and he can become a rabbi, a scholar, the head of a community. His children born after the giyur (for a giyoret — the children she bears) are Jews from birth.

In Orthodox halacha there are a few special laws for gerim. For example, a giyoret cannot marry a kohen (Yevamot 60b; Rambam, Issurei Biah 18:3). Formally, a ger is not considered a relative of his non-Jewish family under the laws of inheritance and marriage, but the sages instituted a number of restrictions so that people would not say he moved from greater holiness to lesser. In such matters always turn to a rabbi.
The mitzvah to love a ger

The Torah speaks many times about how to treat a ger. The Talmud (Bava Metzia 59b) calculates that the warning not to wrong a ger is repeated in the Torah **36 times**, and by another opinion — 46 times. No other mitzvah is repeated so often.

blocks.he: וְגֵר לֹא תוֹנֶה וְלֹא תִלְחָצֶנּוּ, כִּי גֵרִים הֱיִיתֶם בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם
blocks.translit: Ve-ger lo toneh ve-lo tilchatzenu, ki gerim heyitem be'eretz Mitzrayim
blocks.ru: You shall not wrong or oppress the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt

blocks.he: וַאֲהַבְתֶּם אֶת הַגֵּר, כִּי גֵרִים הֱיִיתֶם בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם
blocks.translit: Va'ahavtem et ha-ger, ki gerim heyitem be'eretz Mitzrayim
blocks.ru: You shall love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt

blocks.text: Rambam (De'ot 6:4) explains: loving a ger is **two mitzvot**. A ger is a Jew, and the mitzvah “love your fellow as yourself” applies to him; in addition, there is a separate mitzvah to love the ger. And the Almighty Himself, writes Rambam, “loves the stranger” (Devarim 10:18).
The prohibition of reminding about the past

The Mishnah (Bava Metzia 4:10) counts reminding a person of his past among **onaat devarim** — verbal oppression: one may not say to a penitent “remember your former deeds,” nor to the son of gerim “remember the deeds of your fathers.” All the more so may one not reproach a ger himself with his origin. The Gemara (Bava Metzia 58b) adds: one may not say to a ger who has come to study Torah, “the mouth that ate non-kosher food has come to study Torah given from the mouth of the Almighty.”

blocks.he: אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים
blocks.text: “Verbal oppression” is the prohibition of causing pain with words, including by reminding a person of the past or of non-Jewish origin.

If someone in the community tactlessly asks “who were you before,” you have the right to say gently that this is personal. Whether to share your story is decided by you alone. Often gerim gladly tell of their path, and this inspires others, but there is no obligation to do so.
Connection with family

Giyur does not mean a break with one's parents. Rambam (Mamrim 5:11) writes that a ger is forbidden to curse or strike his non-Jewish father or to humiliate him, so that people will not say: “he went from greater holiness to lesser.” In other words, a ger must **respect his parents** — in truth, even more than is formally required. In practice, gerim visit their families, bring kosher food or dishes with them, explain in advance why they cannot travel on Shabbat, and mark family occasions together, as long as this is not connected with the rites of another religion. Patience and warmth usually help relatives accept your choice in time.

differs.text: In Reform communities the participation of non-Jewish relatives in the life of the community and in the ger’s celebrations is usually encouraged, up to their presence at the giyur ceremony; the extent of participation in non-Jewish family holidays is decided by the ger together with the rabbi.

blocks.text: The hardest thing is usually the religious holidays of one's relatives. The general principle: a ger may come to congratulate the family and share a meal (with attention to kashrut), but does not take part in the rites of another religion. How exactly to act in your situation — discuss it with your rabbi.
Ruth — the model of a giyoret

The Book of Ruth, which is read on Shavuot — the festival of the giving of the Torah — tells of a Moabite woman, a widow, who remained with her mother-in-law Naomi. Naomi three times urges her to return to her people. The other daughter-in-law, Orpah, leaves, but Ruth answers with words that became the eternal formula of giyur:

blocks.he: אַל תִּפְגְּעִי בִי לְעָזְבֵךְ לָשׁוּב מֵאַחֲרָיִךְ, כִּי אֶל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ, וּבַאֲשֶׁר תָּלִינִי אָלִין, עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי
blocks.translit: Al tifge'i vi le'azvekh lashuv me'acharaikh, ki el asher telchi elech, u-va'asher talini alin, amech ami ve'Elohayich Elohai
blocks.ru: Do not urge me to leave you and turn back from you: for wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d.

blocks.text: In these words is everything the beit din asks about: loyalty to the people (“your people shall be my people”), faith (“your G-d my G-d”), readiness to share fate (“where you die, there I will die,” Ruth 1:17). The sages (Yevamot 47b) even derive from the conversation of Naomi and Ruth the laws of how to receive gerim. Ruth's reward is to be the great-grandmother of King David (Ruth 4:17), and thus of the Mashiach from his line. A giyoret stands at the source of Israel's royal dynasty.
Keep on learning
Make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend.

items: Find a regular teacher or rabbi to whom you can bring your questions.
Study regularly, even a little every day: the weekly parashah, the laws, prayer.
Find a chevruta — a study partner.
Stay an active member of the community: prayers, festivals, helping others.
Keep your giyur certificate in a safe place — you will need it for marriage, aliyah, and other occasions.
Many gerim mark the anniversary of their giyur as a personal holiday.

blocks.text: The first years after giyur can be not easy: the euphoria passes, everyday life sets in, along with questions and sometimes loneliness. This is normal. Remember that the whole people of Israel once stood at Sinai just as you stood before the beit din, and said: “Na'aseh venishma — we will do and we will hear.” Welcome home.
Loyalty to the path one has chosen

Giyur is an entry into the covenant forever. A person who, after giyur, adopts another teaching — about G-d who became man, about a Mashiach who has already come, or about replacing the Torah — calls into question the very meaning of his step. By classical halacha, a Jew by birth remains in some respects a Jew even if he has left for another faith, but he departs from the community of the faithful; for a ger, loyalty to the covenant he accepted is the heart of his new life.

If after giyur you are troubled by “almost Jewish” gatherings, holidays “with a different meaning,” or warm invitations without clear teaching, return to your rabbi. Loyalty to the community, to the people, and to the Land of Israel is not a ban on thinking, but a promise you made at the waters of the mikveh.

cards.front: To what is a ger compared, according to Yevamot 22a?
cards.back: To a newborn child: he begins a new life.

cards.front: Does a ger have all the rights of a Jew?
cards.back: Yes: an aliyah to the Torah, the minyan; he can be a rabbi and the head of a community.

cards.front: How many times does the Torah warn not to wrong a ger (Bava Metzia 59b)?
cards.back: 36 times; by another opinion — 46.

cards.front: “Ve-ger lo toneh…” — where is the verse from, and what does it mean?
cards.back: Shemot 22:20: “You shall not wrong or oppress the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt.”

cards.front: Where is the mitzvah to love a ger?
cards.back: Devarim 10:19: “You shall love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

cards.front: Why is love of a ger two mitzvot (Rambam, De'ot 6:4)?
cards.back: He is a Jew (“love your fellow”), and there is a separate mitzvah to love a ger.

cards.front: What is ona'at devarim?
cards.back: Verbal oppression, including reminding a ger of the past or of his origin.

cards.front: Where is the prohibition of reminding the son of gerim of his fathers' deeds?
cards.back: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10.

cards.front: Must a ger respect his non-Jewish parents?
cards.back: Yes: he is forbidden to curse them, strike them, or humiliate them (Rambam, Mamrim 5:11).

cards.front: May a ger take part in the religious rites of his relatives?
cards.back: No; he may congratulate them and share a meal with attention to kashrut, after discussing it with the rabbi.

cards.front: May a giyoret marry a kohen (according to Orthodox halacha)?
cards.back: No (Yevamot 60b; Rambam, Issurei Biah 18:3).

cards.front: What did Ruth say to Naomi (Ruth 1:16)?
cards.back: “Wherever you go, I will go… your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d.”

cards.front: What is Ruth to King David?
cards.back: His great-grandmother: Ruth — Oved — Yishai — David (Ruth 4:17).

cards.front: On which festival is the Book of Ruth read?
cards.back: On Shavuot – the festival of the giving of the Torah.

cards.front: Which teaching of Avot 1:6 is important for a ger after giyur?
cards.back: “Make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend.”

cards.front: Is a ger a relative of his non-Jewish family according to halacha?
cards.back: Formally no: not under the laws of inheritance and marriage. The sages nevertheless imposed restrictions, so that people would not say that he moved from greater holiness to lesser.

cards.front: What is the status of children born to a giyoret after her giyur?
cards.back: They are Jews from birth.

cards.front: What is it forbidden to say to a ger who has come to study Torah?
cards.back: “The mouth that ate non-kosher food has come to study Torah given from the mouth of the Almighty” (Bava Metzia 58b).

cards.front: What is a chevruta?
cards.back: A study partner with whom one learns Torah regularly.

cards.front: Where should the giyur certificate be kept, and why?
cards.back: In a safe place: it will be needed for marriage, aliyah, and other occasions.

cards.front: How do many gerim mark the anniversary of their giyur?
cards.back: As a personal holiday.

cards.front: What did the whole people of Israel say at Sinai, and how is it close to a ger?
cards.back: “Na'aseh venishma — we will do and we will hear”; a ger, like the whole people, begins his path with this answer.

cards.front: What does a ger’s loyalty to the covenant he accepted mean?
cards.back: Not to accept a teaching that replaces G-d, the Mashiach, or the Torah, and in case of doubt to go to one's rabbi rather than decide alone.

lessons.title: Reform giyur: study, community, and beit din
citations: CCAR resolution of 1983 on the Jewish status of a child
Decision of the Supreme Court of Israel, 2021
Giyur school of the “Shaarei Shalom” community (ROOPI)
keyIdeas: Informed choice means study and an honest measure of practice, not a renunciation of the mitzvot for the sake of convenience.
Giyur practice differs: ROOPI and Israel usually require the mikveh and brit milah; North America is more flexible.
A Reform beit din expects a personal story, knowledge, life in the community, and a coherent account of one's covenant.
Civil recognition in Israel and recognition by the Rabbinate are different things; one needs to know this in advance.
After giyur, growth in the community begins: prayer, Shabbat, study, and service — not the end of the path.

blocks.text: Reform, or progressive, giyur is a full path of entry into the Jewish people, not a shortened copy of the Orthodox one. It has its own history, its own documents, its own batei din, and its own seriousness. This lesson gathers it by country and in essence: how the movement understands the Torah and the mitzvot, how a ger is taught and received in North America, in Israel, and in the ROOPI communities, what is asked at the interview, and what begins after the mikveh.
Torah, covenant, and informed choice

Reform Judaism sees in the Torah a sacred revelation inspired by the Almighty, given in history and unfolding in every generation. The Written Torah and the Oral Torah are the heritage of the people, not a museum text. But halacha is not understood as an unchanging legal code that a Jew is obliged to fulfill in its entirety. The mitzvot are a call, a path, and a responsibility. A person enters the **covenant** (brit) consciously: he studies, prays, lives in the community, and himself, honestly, takes upon himself the measure of holiness he is ready to bear.

The principle of **informed choice** is easily misunderstood. It is not permission to do “whatever is more convenient” and not indifference to the law. First one must learn what the tradition says, how the generations lived this mitzvah, how your community understands it — and only then decide how to fulfill it in your own home. “I do not observe it, because in Reform it is allowed” is not a choice, but a refusal to study. “I have studied Shabbat, kashrut, and prayer; this has already become my rhythm, and this is where I am going” — that is Reform seriousness.

From the same root grow the equality of men and women in prayer and in leading the community, openness to gerim, attention to justice and tikkun olam, the readiness to revisit institutions that, in the movement's view, no longer serve human dignity. All of this one must be able to explain in one's own words — calmly, without the argument “who is a real Jew” and without apologizing for one's path.
History: from the 19th century to today's practice

The Reform movement took shape in the 19th century in the German lands and then flourished in North America. The Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR) was founded in 1889, and the World Union for Progressive Judaism (WUPJ) in 1926. The CCAR resolution of 1892 determined that the rites of brit milah and tevilah are not formally required for accepting a ger: the decision was left to the rabbi and the community. This is a historical document, not a full picture of today.

Over the 20th and 21st centuries, practice in many communities became more ritual-centered. An introduction to Judaism (often about a year), a rabbi's mentorship, regular participation in services and festivals, a beit din of three rabbis — this is the usual framework of North American giyur. The mikveh and, for men, brit milah or hatafat dam brit are today often strongly recommended or directly required by a given rabbi, although the formal resolution of 1892 has not been rescinded. Always ask your own community: custom lives in the local places, not only in the old resolution.
Russia, the CIS, and Israel: not a copy of America

In Russia and the CIS countries, progressive giyur is conducted by the **ROOPI** communities, which belong to the WUPJ. According to the description of the giyur school of the St. Petersburg “Shaarei Shalom” community, the path includes a letter of motivation, **no less than a year of study**, regular participation in services, festivals, and the life of the community, an interview before the beit din, and immersion in the mikveh; for men, **brit milah is obligatory**. This is stricter than the minimal North American norm of 1892, and closer to the common Jewish ritual language of transition. The Moscow Center for Progressive Judaism and other ROOPI communities keep their own schools and schedules — find out their rules; do not import someone else's.

In Israel, progressive giyur is conducted by the **Israel Movement for Progressive Judaism** (IMPJ): study, community life, a beit din, and, as a rule, tevilah and brit milah. In 2021 the Supreme Court of Israel ruled that non-Orthodox giyurim performed inside the country are recognized for civil status and under the Law of Return. This is civil recognition. The Chief Rabbinate still does not marry or register such giyurim as a religious status. A person for whom marriage specifically through the Rabbinate matters needs to know this in advance and calmly, without self-deception, choose his path.

items: **North America:** a year of study, the community, a beit din; the mikveh and brit are often recommended or required by the rabbi, although the resolution of 1892 left them to discretion.
**ROOPI / CIS:** a letter, a year of study, regular community life, a beit din, the mikveh; brit milah is obligatory for men.
**Israel (IMPJ):** the movement's program, a beit din, usually the mikveh and brit; civil recognition after 2021, without recognition by the Rabbinate.

blocks.text: The beit din and typical questions

A Reform beit din usually consists of three rabbis of the progressive movement. They are not looking for a reason to refuse and do not set traps, but neither do they go through a formality just for appearance's sake. It is important to them to see that the decision is yours, that you are already living in the people and in the community, that you studied not for an exam, and that you understand which movement you are entering. The questions often sound just as human as in any beit din: why Judaism, why this particular community, how you pray, how you spend Shabbat and the festivals, what you eat, how you will raise children, what Israel and the Jewish people mean to you, what will change after the giyur.

There are also questions specific to the progressive path. What does the covenant mean to you? How do you understand informed choice of the mitzvot — and how are you already applying it? What does prayer look like in your synagogue, which siddur do you use, do you read the Shema and the blessings with understanding? What is tikkun olam for you — not as a slogan, but as a practice? How will the roles in rituals be distributed in your family? Do you know how your movement defines the Jewishness of a child, and how this differs from the Orthodox and Conservative approaches? On these topics you need to have your own words, not a memorized paragraph.

As in any beit din, honesty is valued here above a perfect picture. If something has not yet become your practice, say so: “I am studying this, and here is my next step.” Do not ascribe to yourself an Orthodox observance you do not have, and do not hide behind the phrase “in Reform it is not required.”
Rites of passage and a new name

Where tevilah is part of giyur — and in ROOPI, in Israel, and in many North American communities it is — the immersion remains that same Tanakh language of passing through the waters, as in the other movements. The meaning emphasized by Reform thought is spiritual rebirth and free entry into the covenant. The technical requirements for the mikveh itself may be more flexible than in Orthodox halacha; sometimes immersion takes place in a natural body of water or in a community mikveh. The rabbi guiding you will state the exact procedure.

Whether a man in Progressive giyur has brit milah or hatafat dam brit depends on the country and the rabbi: it is required in ROOPI programs and usually in Israeli Progressive giyur, and in North America it is often expected, although historically it was not always required. A new Jewish name is chosen together with the rabbi; it is announced at the giyur and then used in the community. After emerging from the mikveh, the person is greeted as a Jew: blessings, sometimes “Shehecheyanu,” the embrace of the community. What begins next is not the “end of study” but Jewish life.
Recognition, children, and an honest choice of path

Reform giyur is recognized by Reform communities around the world and by many Conservative ones, especially if there was study, a beit din, a mikveh, and brit milah. The State of Israel recognizes it for the Law of Return (subject to the reservations of ministry practice). Orthodox batei din and the Chief Rabbinate do not recognize it. This is a fact, not a judgment of a person's worth. You need to know it before starting the path, especially if you are thinking of moving, of marriage through the Rabbinate, or of which community your children will live in.

A special case is the 1983 CCAR resolution: a child of **one** Jewish parent — mother or father — is considered a Jew if he or she is being raised in Judaism. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism proceed from the maternal line (and from giyur). A candidate needs to understand this not for the sake of argument but for clarity: how the status of your children will be determined in your community, and how other movements will regard it. If there are already children in the family, the rabbi will discuss in advance whether they will undergo giyur and how they will enter community life.

Choosing a movement is not a contest of strictness. It is a question of which community you want to pray, study, grieve, and rejoice in, which language of the covenant is close to you, and which consequences of recognition you accept. A rabbi will help you see this soberly. Details of the Orthodox and Conservative paths are in the lesson “The Path to Giyur in Different Movements”; this lesson is devoted to telling the Reform path in full.

cards.front: How does Reform Judaism understand the mitzvot?
cards.back: As a sacred path that a Jew studies and consciously accepts; not as a legal code binding in its entirety.

cards.front: What is informed choice?
cards.back: First study the tradition, listen to the community and your conscience, then honestly decide how to fulfill the mitzvot in your life.

cards.front: What did the CCAR rule about giyur in 1892?
cards.back: That brit milah and tevilah are not formally required for giyur; the rabbi and the community determine the procedure.

cards.front: What does giyur in North America usually look like today?
cards.back: A year of study, life in the community, a beit din of three rabbis; the mikveh and brit milah or hatafat dam brit are often strongly recommended or required by the rabbi.

cards.front: What does the ROOPI giyur school require, according to the description by “Shaarei Shalom”?
cards.back: A letter of motivation, at least a year of study, regular participation in community life, a beit din and a mikveh; for men, brit milah is required.

cards.front: Who conducts Progressive giyur in Russia and the CIS?
cards.back: ROOPI communities, which belong to the World Union for Progressive Judaism (WUPJ).

cards.front: Who conducts Progressive giyur in Israel?
cards.back: The Israel Movement for Progressive Judaism (IMPJ) with its own batei din and study programs.

cards.front: Does the Law of Return recognize Reform giyur?
cards.back: Yes, provided the conditions of the law are met: both giyur performed abroad and, after the 2021 Supreme Court decision, Progressive giyur within Israel — for civil status.

cards.front: Does the Chief Rabbinate of Israel recognize Reform giyur?
cards.back: No. Religious marriage and status through the Rabbinate require an Orthodox giyur under its control.

cards.front: Who usually makes up a Reform beit din?
cards.back: Three rabbis of the Progressive movement; sometimes your own community's rabbi and invited colleagues are included.

cards.front: What is expected first and foremost at a Reform interview?
cards.back: An honest personal story, knowledge, active participation in the community, and a clear account of how you are already living as a Jew.
