cards.front: What is the 1983 CCAR resolution on the Jewishness of a child?
cards.back: A child of one Jewish parent — mother or father — is considered a Jew if he or she is being raised as a Jew. Orthodox and Masorti Judaism do not accept this.

cards.front: Why does a candidate need to know about patrilineality even if he himself is a ger?
cards.back: In order to understand whom his community considers a Jew, how this will affect his children, and why other movements decide differently.

cards.front: What remains common to giyur in all movements?
cards.back: Serious intention, study, connection with the community and the people, an interview, and — in most programs — rites of passage.

cards.front: How do Reform communities regard the mikveh in giyur today?
cards.back: In ROOPI and in Israel tevilah is part of giyur; in North America some rabbis require it, some strongly recommend it, and some leave it as a strong custom.

cards.front: What happens after Reform giyur?
cards.back: The person becomes a Jew of his or her community and movement: continuing study, prayer, festivals, and service, growing in the covenant all his or her life.

cards.front: Can Reform giyur be considered “easier”?
cards.back: No. It differs in its understanding of obligation, but it requires study, honesty, community life, and a well-considered personal path.

cards.front: What is the WUPJ?
cards.back: The World Union for Progressive Judaism — an international association of Reform, Liberal, and Progressive communities.

cards.front: What should you ask yourself when choosing a Reform beit din?
cards.back: Which community do I want to live and raise children in? Am I prepared for how different movements will recognize this giyur? Does my path match the path of this community?

cards.front: How should you speak about the mitzvot at a Reform beit din?
cards.back: Not “anything goes for me,” but “I have studied; this is what I already keep, this is where I am heading, and here is why it is holy to me.”

cards.front: Do Conservative communities recognize Reform giyur?
cards.back: Many do, especially if there was study, a beit din, a mikveh, and — for men — brit milah; the final decision depends on the community.

cards.front: Why is there a year of community life in Reform giyur?
cards.back: So that Jewishness becomes not a subject for examination but the rhythm of the week: prayer, Shabbat, festivals, people, and service.

questions.prompt: How many judges are required for a beit din for giyur?
options: One rabbi
Two witnesses
Three
Ten (a minyan)
questions.explanation: The Talmud rules: “a ger requires three” — as does any court of Jewish law.
questions.source: Talmud, Yevamot 46b

questions.prompt: Through which three things, according to Rambam, did the people of Israel enter the covenant?
options: Prayer, fasting, and charity
Circumcision, immersion, and a sacrifice
Shabbat, kashrut, and tefillin
Study, repentance, and festivals
questions.explanation: From this Rambam derives the order of giyur in all generations: milah, tevilah, and (in the time of the Temple) a korban.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:1–4

questions.prompt: According to the Talmud, what is the first question asked of someone who comes to become Jewish?
options: “Do you know Hebrew?”
“Who are your parents?”
“What have you seen that you have come to become Jewish? Do you not know that Israel is suffering now?”
“Are you ready to move to the Land of Israel?”
questions.explanation: In this way the beit din checks whether the candidate understands that he or she is sharing the fate of the people.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47a

questions.prompt: According to the Talmud, before accepting a candidate the beit din must enumerate for him in detail all 613 mitzvot and their particulars.
questions.explanation: They tell him of some of the lenient and some of the strict mitzvot, “without burdening him excessively or being punctilious.”
questions.source: Talmud, Yevamot 47a–b

questions.prompt: A non-Jew who agrees to accept the whole Torah except for one mitzvah is not accepted for giyur.
questions.explanation: Kabbalat mitzvot means accepting the system of mitzvot in its entirety.
questions.source: Talmud, Bechorot 30b

questions.prompt: What is the acceptance of the mitzvot by the candidate before the beit din called? (two words)
questions.explanation: Kabbalat mitzvot is the heart of giyur.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:3

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: “Do you know that giyur is not needed in order to be a good person in the eyes of the Almighty? Then why have you come?” Answer as the candidate.
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “Yes, I know that a righteous person of the nations of the world, who keeps the seven Noahide Laws, has a share in the World to Come. I have come not for salvation but because I feel that my place is among the people of Israel. Over the years of study the Torah has become for me not just a book but a way of life: Shabbat, prayer, community. I want to be obligated by the mitzvot, not merely to admire them from the sidelines, and I want to pass this life on to my children.”
keyPoints: Understanding that Judaism does not require giyur of non-Jews (the seven Noahide Laws)
Giyur is the acceptance of obligations, not “salvation”
A personal, specific motivation
A desire to belong to the people and the covenant
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands the essence of giyur as the acceptance of obligations.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11; Issurei Biah 14:1

questions.prompt: “Do you not know that the Jewish people suffers and is persecuted?” How would you answer this ancient question today?
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I know. I have read the history of the pogroms and the Shoah, and I see antisemitism today as well. It is not a matter of indifference to me, and at times I am afraid. But I do not want to be with the people only in good times. As Ruth said to Naomi: ‘Your people shall be my people.’ I consider it an honor to share with it both its joys and its hardships.”
keyPoints: An honest acknowledgment of the reality of antisemitism
A conscious readiness to share the fate of the people
A connection with the Talmud's answer “I know, and I am not worthy” or with the words of Ruth
Without bravado and without minimizing
questions.explanation: This question is from Yevamot 47a; the right answer is conscious consent to share the fate of the people.
questions.source: Talmud, Yevamot 47a; Rut 1:16

questions.prompt: Who, according to Orthodox halacha, may serve as a judge in a beit din for giyur?
options: Any three Jews, including the candidate's relatives
Three observant Jews, fit to serve as witnesses and not related to the candidate or to one another
One rabbi and any two witnesses, including non-Jews
Only the country's Chief Rabbi
questions.explanation: The judges must be valid witnesses and not related by kinship.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:3

questions.prompt: What does “kabbalat mitzvot” mean to you? Why is giyur invalid without it?
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “Kabbalat mitzvot is my promise before the beit din that I accept the mitzvot upon myself as an obligation, not as a voluntary hobby. Without it, the mikveh and brit are only water and an operation: Jewishness is a covenant, and a covenant means obligations. I understand that I do not know everything and will make mistakes, but I am ready to learn all my life and to make decisions in accordance with the Torah and the guidance of a rabbi.”
keyPoints: The acceptance of the mitzvot as an obligation
Kabbalat mitzvot is the heart of giyur; without it the rites have no effect
A readiness to learn, not a claim to know everything
An understanding of the position of one's own movement
questions.explanation: According to halacha, the acceptance of the mitzvot is an integral and central part of giyur.
questions.source: Talmud, Bechorot 30b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:3

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, kabbalat mitzvot is a commitment to live a Jewish life, to study, and to make an informed choice about observance — not the acceptance of the whole of halacha as binding law.

questions.prompt: What does the story of Hillel and the non-Jew who asked to be taught the Torah “while standing on one foot” teach?
options: That giyur should be done quickly, without study
That a sincere person should be drawn close patiently, and then — “go and study”
That non-Jews may not be taught the Torah
That it is enough to know one mitzvah
questions.explanation: Hillel stated the main principle and added: “the rest is commentary; go and study.”
questions.source: Talmud, Shabbat 31a

questions.prompt: Match each movement with its approach to giyur.
pairs: Full observance of halacha before giyur, life near the community
Binding halacha as interpreted by the movement's rabbis
Letter of motivation, ≥1 year of study, participation in the community
questions.explanation: All three movements require study and a beit din, but they understand the bindingness of the mitzvot differently.
questions.source: “Giyur in the Context of the Different Denominations of Judaism”; reformspb.ru/giura

questions.prompt: How long does the path to Orthodox giyur usually take?
options: A few days
About a month
As a rule, from one to three years
At least ten years
questions.explanation: The length depends on the person and the beit din; the candidate must have time to begin living an observant life.
questions.source: orthodox-conversion.com: “Orthodox and Conservative Giyur”

questions.prompt: What is NOT among the requirements of ROOPI Progressive giyur according to the “Shaarei Shalom” school?
options: A letter of motivation
At least a year of study
Participation in community life
Mandatory residence in Israel
questions.explanation: Residence in Israel is not a condition for giyur.
questions.source: The “Shaarei Shalom” giyur school, reformspb.ru/giura

questions.prompt: According to ROOPI rules, brit milah for men is required in giyur.
questions.explanation: This is stated on the page of the “Shaarei Shalom” giyur school; in North American Reform Judaism the rules are different.
questions.source: The “Shaarei Shalom” giyur school, reformspb.ru/giura

questions.prompt: Which giyur is recognized by all movements of Judaism?
options: Reform
Conservative
Orthodox
Any giyur performed in Israel
questions.explanation: The non-Orthodox movements recognize Orthodox giyur; the reverse is not true.
questions.source: orthodox-conversion.com; EJE, article “Proselytes”

questions.prompt: Recognition of giyur for the Law of Return automatically grants the right to marry through the Chief Rabbinate of Israel.
questions.explanation: Civil recognition and religious recognition are different things; the Rabbinate recognizes only an Orthodox giyur approved by it.
questions.source: Law of Return (1950, amendment 1970); EJE

questions.prompt: Who is considered a Jew for the purposes of the Law of Return after the 1970 amendment?
options: Only one born to a Jewish father
One born to a Jewish mother, or who has undergone giyur and does not profess another religion
Anyone who knows Hebrew
Only one who has undergone an Orthodox giyur in Israel
questions.explanation: The 1970 amendment introduced this definition and extended the right of repatriation to the children and grandchildren of Jews and to their spouses.
questions.source: Law of Return, 1970 amendment (EJE)

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: “Why did you choose this particular community and this movement?” Answer honestly.
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I visited different synagogues, and it was here that I felt this was my community: the way people pray and study here, the way the mitzvot are understood here, is close to me. I spoke with the rabbi about the differences between the movements, and I understand that not everyone will recognize my giyur equally. I made this decision consciously, and I intend to raise my children in this community.”
keyPoints: Knowledge of the differences between the movements
A conscious choice, not an accident
Understanding the issues of recognition
A connection with a specific community and rabbi
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to be sure that the choice of movement is conscious and connected to real life in a community.
questions.source: “Giyur in the Context of the Different Denominations of Judaism”

questions.prompt: An Orthodox beit din asks: “Where do you live, and how do you get to the synagogue on Shabbat?” What is important to say?
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “Six months ago I moved closer to the community; now the synagogue is a fifteen-minute walk away. On Shabbat I do not use transport, and I come to the evening and morning prayers. If that is not yet the case, I will say what steps I plan to take rather than make things up.”
keyPoints: Driving is forbidden on Shabbat — you need to live within walking distance
Regular participation in the prayers
Honesty about the actual state of affairs
A readiness to change one's life for the sake of observance
questions.explanation: Orthodox giyur presupposes life near the community, since driving is forbidden on Shabbat.
questions.source: orthodox-conversion.com: “Orthodox and Conservative Giyur”

questions.prompt: Conservative (Masorti) giyur includes mandatory tevilah and, for men, brit milah or hatafat dam brit.
questions.explanation: Masorti considers these rites halachically binding.
questions.source: Masorti/Rabbinical Assembly (Derakhim overview)

questions.prompt: “If some communities do not recognize your giyur — how will you relate to that?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I know about this in advance: the rabbi explained to me which communities and institutions recognize this giyur and which do not. It pains me to think that someone will not consider me a Jew, but I understand that this is a question of different understandings of halacha. My decision does not change because of this: I will live a Jewish life and respect other Jews even if they do not recognize me.”
keyPoints: Knowledge of the facts about recognition
Calm and respect for the other movements
Firmness of decision
An understanding of the consequences for marriage and children
questions.explanation: The beit din checks that the candidate understands the consequences of his or her choice.
questions.source: “Giyur in the Context of the Different Denominations of Judaism”; orthodox-conversion.com

questions.prompt: What matters most at the beit din interview?
options: To know all 39 categories of work on Shabbat by heart
Honesty and sincerity in the answers
To say what the judges want to hear
To answer as briefly as possible, in a single word
questions.explanation: Knowledge matters, but the beit din above all checks sincerity; exaggerations destroy trust.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:14

questions.prompt: “Why do you want to become a Jew?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “It all began when I first spent a Shabbat with friends: I was struck that an entire day could be devoted not to work but to family, prayer, and meaning. Then I began reading the Torah and realized that these questions — about G-d, about justice, about duty to other people — had always been mine. For two years now I have been going to the community and living by the Jewish calendar. I cannot imagine my life outside this people.”
keyPoints: A personal story, not general words
What specifically in Judaism matters to you
Real practice that has already entered your life
A connection with the people, not only with ideas
questions.explanation: This is the main question of giyur since the time of the Talmud (“What have you seen?”).
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47a

questions.prompt: “Your partner is Jewish. Are you undergoing giyur for the sake of marriage?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “Yes, it was through my partner that I came to know Judaism, and I do not hide this. But over the course of study it has become my own path: I study, pray, and keep Shabbat not for his or her sake but because I believe. If, G-d forbid, our relationship were to end, I would still remain in the community and continue on the path to giyur.”
keyPoints: To honestly acknowledge the partner's role
To show one's own, independent motivation
Specific examples of personal practice
An understanding that Rambam (13:14) requires such cases to be examined
questions.explanation: Rambam requires checking whether a person is coming for the sake of marriage; honesty matters most here.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:14

questions.prompt: “What do you believe? Tell us about your faith in G-d.”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I believe in the One G-d, the Creator of the world, who has no image or body and to whom alone one must pray. I believe that He gave the Torah to the people of Israel and that how we live matters to Him. I no longer belong to the religion in which I grew up, and I do not take part in its rituals. There are moments of doubt, but I look for answers in study and prayer.”
keyPoints: The unity of the Almighty and the renunciation of idolatry
A break with the former religion
The Torah as the gift of the Almighty
Honesty about doubts without abandoning the fundamentals
questions.explanation: Rambam requires explaining to the candidate in detail the unity of the Almighty and the prohibition of idolatry.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 14:2

differs.text: In a Reform beit din a broader theological understanding of G-d and Revelation is allowed; what matters is the sincerity of the search and the renunciation of another religion.

questions.prompt: “You grew up in another faith. How do you relate to it now?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I grew up in another faith, and I respect my loved ones. But I understand and accept that in Judaism no human being is G-d or Mashiach, and Mashiach has not yet come. I believe only in the One G-d, I pray to no one but Him, and I do not take part in my former rituals. My faith is now bound only to the Torah.”
keyPoints: Unambiguously: no human being is G-d; Mashiach has not yet come
Respect for the family without taking part in the rituals
Monotheism, and prayer to the Almighty alone
The absence of “double faith”
questions.explanation: The beit din must be sure that the candidate has fully renounced his former religion.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 14:2; Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: “Tell us how your Shabbat goes.”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “On Friday afternoon I prepare the food in advance, and before sunset I light the candles. I go to the synagogue to welcome Shabbat, then at home I say kiddush over the wine and bless the challot. I turn off my phone and computer for the whole of Shabbat. In the morning — prayer and Torah reading; in the afternoon, a meal and study; in the evening, havdalah. It is still hard for me not to check my email, but I am managing.”
keyPoints: A concrete description: candles, kiddush, challot, prayer, havdalah
Refraining from work and (depending on the movement) from electronics
A connection with the community
Honesty about difficulties
questions.explanation: A description of a real Shabbat convinces more than a retelling of the rules.
questions.source: Shemot 20:8–11; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 72

differs.text: In a Reform community it is important to show how you observe Shabbat meaningfully; the prohibitions of halacha are observed as a matter of personal choice.

questions.prompt: “How is your kitchen set up? What do you do if you make a mistake and put a meat spoon into a dairy pot?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I have two sinks or separate basins, separate sets of dishes, towels, and sponges for meat and for dairy, and a third set for pareve. I buy only products with a reliable kashrut symbol. If I mix up the dishes, especially hot ones, I do not decide on my own: I set them aside and call the rabbi, because the answer depends on whether the dishes and the food were hot. Between meat and dairy I wait according to the custom of our community.”
keyPoints: Separate dishes for meat and dairy
Reliable kashrut of the food
In doubtful cases — a question to the rabbi
Waiting between meat and dairy according to custom
questions.explanation: An Orthodox beit din expects practical knowledge of the laws of kashrut and the ability to ask the rabbi a question.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 46

questions.prompt: “How did your parents react to your decision? How will you keep in touch with them after giyur?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “At first my mother was afraid that I was growing distant from her. I talked with her many times and invited her to a festival in the community. Now she has accepted my decision, although she does not understand everything. I will visit my parents; I bring kosher food with me, and I come to their holidays to congratulate them, but I do not take part in the rituals. I am obligated to respect my parents, and Judaism requires this of me.”
keyPoints: Respect for parents (Rambam, Mamrim 5:11)
Thought-out practical decisions (food, Shabbat, holidays)
Firmness of the decision while keeping the warmth
Honesty about difficulties
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate has thought through the family difficulties.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Mamrim 5:11

questions.prompt: “You have children from a non-Jewish marriage. How do you see their Jewish future?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I know that my giyur does not automatically make my children who were already born into Jews. We discussed with the rabbi the possibility of giyur for them, and I understand that for this they need to grow up in a Jewish home and study in the community. If their father is opposed, I will respect his rights, but I will give the children as much of a Jewish upbringing as I can.”
keyPoints: Children born before the mother’s giyur do not automatically become Jews (Orthodox/Conservative)
The giyur of minors is by decision of the beit din
A Jewish upbringing at home
Respect for the other parent
questions.explanation: According to halacha, the status of children is determined by the mother at the moment of birth; those born before the giyur need a separate giyur.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 11a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:7

differs.text: In Reform Judaism in North America, a child of one Jewish parent who is being raised as a Jew may be considered a Jew without a separate giyur; in ROOPI, check the rules with your rabbi.

questions.prompt: “How do you take part in the life of the community?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I go to prayers on Shabbat and on the festivals, and on Tuesdays I study in a group on the weekly parashah. On Chanukah I helped prepare a celebration for the children, and on Pesach I helped put together food packages for the elderly. I know many people in the community, and it matters to me to be part of it, not a guest. After giyur I want to continue volunteering.”
keyPoints: Regular participation in prayers and festivals
Study in the community
Help and tzedakah
The wish to be part of it, not a guest
questions.explanation: Judaism is a religion of community; the beit din wants to see real involvement.
questions.source: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (Hillel: “Do not separate yourself from the community”)

questions.prompt: “What do you not yet observe, or what is hardest for you?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “What is hardest for me is daily prayer: in the morning I am often in a hurry and recite only the Shema and short blessings. I have agreed with the rabbi that I will gradually add parts of the prayer. It is also hard for me when I visit colleagues where there is no kosher food — now I let them know in advance and bring something with me.”
keyPoints: Honestly name a real difficulty
Show a plan and progress
Rely on the rabbi’s advice
Neither exaggerate nor understate
questions.explanation: An honest answer about weak points inspires more trust than a claim of flawlessness.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47a (“they do not burden excessively”)

questions.prompt: If at the interview you do not know the answer to a question, it is better to confidently make something up than to admit it.
questions.explanation: An honest “I do not know, but I will find out” is respected; a made-up answer undermines trust in the candidate.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:14 (a check of sincerity)

questions.prompt: Which answer to the question about motivation is the beit din most likely to consider insufficient?
options: “Shabbat and Torah study have become the center of my life”
“I want to raise children in the Jewish community where I already live”
“I need giyur in order to get the documents processed faster”
“I feel that the people of Israel are my people”
questions.explanation: External reasons (documents, gain) are exactly what the beit din checks, according to the Rambam.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:14

questions.prompt: “Why will you not remain a righteous person of the nations of the world, keeping the seven Noahide Laws?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I respect this path and I know that it is a real one. But I want not only to keep the laws common to all humanity, but to be part of the covenant of Israel: to pray together with the community, to keep Shabbat as a Jew, and to bear responsibility for the people. For me this is not a question of reward, but a question of who I am.”
keyPoints: Knowledge of the seven Noahide Laws
Giyur is the acceptance of obligations
The desire to belong to the covenant and to the people
The motive is not reward
questions.explanation: The question checks the understanding that giyur is not the only path to righteousness.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11

questions.prompt: “Do you believe that the Oral Torah was given at Sinai and that halacha is binding for you?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “Yes. I believe that the Almighty gave Moshe at Sinai both the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, and that without the Oral Torah one cannot understand the Written Torah — for example, how to make tefillin, or what is forbidden on Shabbat. I accept halacha as binding, and when I do not know how to act, I ask the rabbi.”
keyPoints: The divine origin of the Written and the Oral Torah
Halacha is binding
An example of the connection between the Oral and the Written Torah
A readiness to ask the rabbi
questions.explanation: Orthodox giyur requires accepting the Torah and halacha in full, including the Oral Torah.
questions.source: Rambam, the 13 principles of faith (the 8th and the 9th); Bechorot 30b

questions.prompt: What is a chatzitzah?
options: The blessing after immersion
A barrier between the body and the mikveh water
A document of the giyur
A woman who assists at the women’s mikveh
questions.explanation: Anything that separates the body from the water (jewelry, nail polish, dirt) can make the tevilah invalid.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 198

questions.prompt: Why does the ger recite the blessing “al ha-tevilah” after the immersion, and not before it?
options: It is faster that way
Before the immersion he is not yet a Jew and cannot say “who has commanded us”
Because a blessing is forbidden to be said in the water at all
Because that is what one does with any mitzvah
questions.explanation: Only after emerging from the water as a Jew can the ger give thanks for the mitzvah that now obligates him.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:2

questions.prompt: What water is fit for a kosher mikveh?
options: Any tap water poured from a hose
Natural water (rain or spring) that came in by itself, and was not drawn into vessels
Sea water only
Water sanctified by a rabbi
questions.explanation: The laws of the mikveh are derived from Vayikra 11:36: “a spring and a pool, a gathering of waters.”
questions.source: Vayikra 11:36; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 201

questions.prompt: The tevilah of a ger may be performed at night or on Shabbat, if that is more convenient for the beit din.
questions.explanation: The tevilah of a ger is an act of the court, and a court does not sit at night, on Shabbat, or on festivals.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46b; Rambam, Issurei Biah 13:7

questions.prompt: What is the full immersion in a mikveh that completes giyur called?
questions.explanation: Tevilah is the immersion of the whole body all at once.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46b–47b

questions.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: A pool of natural water of no less than 40 seah
A barrier between the body and the water
A woman who assists at the immersion
questions.explanation: These are the basic terms connected with the mikveh.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 198, 201, 268

questions.prompt: Tell us how you will prepare for the tevilah and how it will proceed.
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “In advance I will trim and clean my nails, remove nail polish and jewelry, and take out my contact lenses. Before the immersion I will take a shower, wash my hair, and comb it, so that no chatzitzah remains. I will enter the water in the presence of the beit din, confirm once again that I accept the mitzvot, and immerse completely — so that my hair too is under the water. When I come out, I will say the blessing “al ha-tevilah,” immerse once more, and, by custom, say “Shehecheyanu.””
keyPoints: Removing the chatzitzah: jewelry, nail polish, lenses, dirt
A shower, and washing and combing the hair
Accepting the mitzvot again before the judges
Full immersion of the whole body and the hair
The blessing after immersion
questions.explanation: The beit din may check whether the candidate understands the order of the tevilah.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 198; 268:2

questions.prompt: At a woman’s tevilah the judges of the beit din do not look at her body: a woman assists her, and the judges stand outside or enter when she is covered by the water.
questions.explanation: This is how the Talmud describes it, and this order is kept for the sake of modesty.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47b

questions.prompt: What is performed at giyur for a man who is already circumcised for medical reasons?
options: Nothing; that is enough
A second full circumcision
Hatafat dam brit — the drawing of a drop of the blood of the covenant
Tevilah only, without a mohel taking part
questions.explanation: The circumcision was not performed for the sake of the covenant, so a drop of the blood of the covenant is drawn.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 135a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1

questions.prompt: What is the specialist who performs brit milah called?
questions.explanation: A mohel knows the laws of milah; for adults this is often a physician-mohel.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 264

questions.prompt: How does a ger’s patronymic usually sound in a Jewish name?
options: By the name of the non-Jewish father
“Ben (bat) Avraham avinu”; in many communities — “ben (bat) Avraham ve-Sarah”
“Ben (bat) Moshe Rabbeinu”
A ger has no patronymic
questions.explanation: A ger is considered a son or daughter of the forefather Avraham.
questions.source: Rambam, Letter to Ovadyah the Ger; the custom of the communities

questions.prompt: Match the concept with its source.
pairs: Avraham’s circumcision at the age of 99
A drop of the blood of the covenant for one already circumcised
questions.explanation: Knowing the sources helps one understand the meaning of the rites.
questions.source: Bereshit 17; Shabbat 135a; Yevamot 47b

questions.prompt: “Does brit milah in adulthood frighten you? Why are you ready for it?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “Honestly, it is a little frightening. I spoke with the mohel; I know that it is done under anesthesia and that healing will take several weeks. But for me this is the sign of the covenant that the Almighty made with Avraham, and Avraham himself did this at the age of 99. I want this sign to be on me as well.”
keyPoints: Honesty about the fear
Knowledge of the practical side (mohel, anesthesia, healing)
The meaning: the sign of Avraham’s covenant (Bereshit 17)
Readiness that comes from faith
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to see that the candidate understands the meaning of milah and is ready for it consciously.
questions.source: Bereshit 17:10, 17:24

questions.prompt: What is the drawing of a drop of the blood of the covenant from an already circumcised ger called? (three words)
questions.explanation: This is a symbolic circumcision for the sake of the covenant.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1

questions.prompt: According to the Talmud, what is a ger who has accepted Judaism like?
options: A guest in the house
A newborn infant
A hired worker
A resident of another country
questions.explanation: “A ger who has accepted Judaism is like a newborn infant” — he begins a new life.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 22a

questions.prompt: Whose story, read on Shavuot, is considered the model of giyur? (a name)
questions.explanation: Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi: “Your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d.”
questions.source: Ruth 1:16

questions.prompt: Match the source with its content.
pairs: Do not wrong a ger or oppress him
Do not remind him of his fathers’ deeds
questions.explanation: The Torah and the Sages repeatedly require that one love the ger and treat him with care.
questions.source: Shemot 22:20; Devarim 10:19; Mishnah, Bava Metzia 4:10; Rut 4:17

questions.prompt: “What will you do after giyur so as not to stop growing?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “I understand that giyur is not a finish line but a beginning. I will continue to study with the rabbi once a week and to learn the weekly parashah. I want to find a chavruta and, in a year, begin to study the Mishnah. I will stay in the community and help at the festivals. As it is said in Avot: “Make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend.””
keyPoints: Giyur is a beginning, not an end
A steady teacher and regular study
A chavruta and the community
Concrete plans
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to see that the candidate will continue Jewish life after giyur.
questions.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6

questions.prompt: What, according to the Rambam, is forbidden to a ger with regard to his non-Jewish father?
options: To visit him
To speak with him
To curse, strike, and humiliate him
To accept gifts from him
questions.explanation: A ger must respect his parents, so that people will not say that he has passed from a greater holiness to a lesser one.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Mamrim 5:11

questions.prompt: “How do you understand Ruth’s words, “Your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d,” as they apply to you?”
questions.modelAnswer: Sample answer — speak in your own words and honestly: “For me these words have two parts, and both matter. “Your people are my people” — I bind my fate to the Jews, to their joys and their troubles. “Your G-d is my G-d” — I accept the faith and the mitzvot. Ruth did not know everything, but she was faithful to the end — “where you die, there I too will die.” I do not know everything either, but I choose this path forever.”
keyPoints: Two sides: the people and the faith
Faithfulness and the finality of the choice (Rut 1:17)
Ruth as the model of a giyoret
A personal application
questions.explanation: The words of Ruth are the classic formula of giyur; the Sages derive from them the laws of accepting gerim.
questions.source: Rut 1:16–17; Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47b

questions.prompt: “What does immersion in the mikveh mean to you? Why is it tevilah that completes giyur?”
questions.modelAnswer: For me, tevilah is the moment when preparation becomes reality: I enter the water still a non-Jew, and I come out a Jew. I understand that it is the immersion that completes giyur, and I want to go through it calmly, with full attention, and not as a formality. Before the immersion I will confirm once again before the judges that I accept the mitzvot, and I will make sure that the water covers my whole body and my hair. When I come out of the water, I will say the blessing “al ha-tevilah”: only once I have become a Jew can I say “who has commanded us.”
keyPoints: Tevilah completes giyur: on coming out of the water a person becomes a Jew
Before the immersion one accepts the mitzvot once more; the water covers the whole body and the hair
The blessing is said after the immersion, when one is already a Jew
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to hear that the candidate understands the meaning of tevilah as the completion of giyur, and does not regard it as a formal procedure.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:6–7; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:2

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, tevilah is understood as a spiritual symbol of transition; in the communities of ROOPI and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it.

questions.prompt: “Do you have fillings, a tattoo, or a medical device? What will you do about this before the immersion?”
questions.modelAnswer: I have several permanent fillings, and I told the rabbi about this in advance, so that the question would be settled before the day of giyur and not in the mikveh itself. I know that many fillings, crowns, and tattoos are not considered a chatzitzah, but I do not want to decide this myself. The main condition of tevilah is that there be nothing between the body and the water. So on the day of the immersion I will wash thoroughly, comb my hair, remove jewelry and lenses, take off the nail polish, and trim my nails short. If the mikveh attendant notices something, I will calmly correct it before the immersion.
keyPoints: A chatzitzah is a barrier between the body and the water
Fillings, crowns, tattoos, and medical devices are discussed with the rabbi in advance; many of them are not considered a chatzitzah
Preparation: a shower, hair combed, jewelry, lenses, and nail polish removed
questions.explanation: The judges check that the candidate knows about a chatzitzah and will take the preparation seriously, and settles difficult cases with the rabbi in advance.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 198; 268:2–3

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, tevilah is understood as a spiritual symbol of transition; in the communities of ROOPI and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it.

questions.prompt: “What Jewish name have you chosen, and why?”
questions.modelAnswer: I chose the name Ruth and discussed it with the rabbi in advance. Ruth, a Moabite, left her people and said to Naomi: “Your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d.” This path is very close to mine. I will be called “Rut bat Avraham avinu”: Avraham is the father of gerim, and for me he is a father in the people of Israel. This name will be with me all my life: in the ketubah, in prayers for me, and wherever the community uses a Jewish name.
keyPoints: The name is chosen in advance together with the rabbi
A ger’s name takes the form “ben/bat Avraham avinu”
It is good to explain the personal meaning of the choice, and the connection with a hero of the Tanakh
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at whether the choice of name has been thought through, and whether the candidate understands that he or she becomes a son or daughter of Avraham.
questions.source: The custom of giving a name to a ger; Rambam, Letter to Ovadyah the Ger

questions.prompt: “You were already circumcised in childhood. Why, then, do you need hatafat dam brit?”
questions.modelAnswer: I was circumcised in childhood for medical reasons, and it was not done for the sake of the covenant. Brit milah is the sign of the Almighty’s covenant with Avraham, so for giyur it matters that the circumcision be performed specifically for the sake of entering the covenant. Halacha rules that a drop of the blood of the covenant be drawn from me — hatafat dam brit; it is a short and almost painless procedure. For me it means that I am entering the covenant of Avraham, although the earlier circumcision was not such a covenant.
keyPoints: The earlier circumcision was not performed for the sake of the covenant
Hatafat dam brit — the drawing of a drop of the blood of the covenant
Source: Shabbat 135a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1
questions.explanation: The judges check whether the candidate understands that brit is a covenant, and not a medical fact.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 135a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1

differs.text: In the Reform movement of North America, brit milah for an adult ger is formally not obligatory; in ROOPI and in Progressive giyur in Israel it is part of the procedure.

questions.prompt: “Your relatives celebrate their own religious holidays and invite you. What will you do after giyur?”
questions.modelAnswer: I love my parents very much, and I do not want my giyur to look like a break with the family: respecting them is my obligation after giyur as well. I will come to congratulate them, spend time with them, and share the meal if I can keep kashrut — for example, I will bring my own kosher food. But I will not take part in the rituals of another religion, and I will gently explain to them in advance why. If the situation is complicated, I will consult my rabbi.
keyPoints: Respect for parents continues (Rambam, Mamrim 5:11)
One may congratulate them and share the meal, with kashrut kept in mind
Do not take part in the rituals of another religion; disputed cases — to the rabbi
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to see a combination of warmth toward the family and firmness on the question of another religion’s worship.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels (Mamrim) 5:11

differs.text: In Reform communities, the participation of non-Jewish relatives in the life of the community and in the ger’s festivals is encouraged; the ger, together with the rabbi, sets the boundaries of participation in non-Jewish family holidays.

questions.prompt: What did the word “ger” originally mean in the Tanakh?
options: A slave bought from idolaters
A sojourner living among strangers
The High Priest in the Temple
A warrior who served the king
questions.explanation: The lesson says: in the Tanakh the word “ger” originally meant “sojourner,” “one living among strangers,” and in the language of the Sages it came to mean one who has entered the people of Israel and accepted its Torah.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is the Giyur Beit Din

questions.prompt: From which word, said about the ger in the Torah, do the Sages derive that giyur is performed before a court of three?
options: Mishpat
Tzedakah
Teshuvah
Brit
questions.explanation: The Sages derive this from the verse where the word “mishpat” — “law,” “judgment” — is said about the ger: any legal case is heard by a panel of no fewer than three (Yevamot 46b).
questions.source: Bamidbar 15:15–16; Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46b

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Forbidden Relations 13:14), what does the beit din find out about the candidate before accepting them?
options: Whether he knows the tractate Yevamot by heart
Whether he has Jewish ancestors up to the seventh generation
Whether he is coming not for money, status, out of fear, or for the sake of marriage
Whether he will be able to move to the Land of Israel in the future
questions.explanation: The Rambam explains: the beit din finds out whether an external reason brought the person; if the reason is external, giyur is postponed; if it is sincere, they are accepted.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:14

questions.prompt: What happens to a ger who stops observing the mitzvot after giyur?
options: His giyur is automatically annulled
He returns to the status of a non-Jew
He must be accepted into giyur all over again
He remains a Jew, though an apostate
questions.explanation: According to Yevamot 47b, such a person is an apostate Jew, but a Jew all the same: giyur is not revoked even if the person later stops observing.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46b–47b

questions.prompt: According to the Torah, after giyur the same Torah and the same law apply to the ger as to a Jew by birth.
questions.explanation: The verse Bamidbar 15:16 teaches: “One Torah and one law shall be for you and for the stranger” — a ger is not a “second-class Jew,” but a full member of the people.
questions.source: Bamidbar 15:15–16

differs.text: In Reform Judaism the ger is a full member of the people, but kabbalat mitzvot is the acceptance of the Jewish faith, destiny, and life of the community, and a commitment to learn and to observe consciously; the person chooses individual mitzvot and deepens them on their own, rather than accepting all of halacha as binding law.

questions.prompt: A strict law requires refusing the giyur candidate three times before accepting them.
questions.explanation: There is no strict law of three refusals: it is a custom of a number of communities, which grew out of the Talmud's idea of testing sincerity.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is the Giyur Beit Din

questions.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: A righteous ger in traditional texts
A person who has undergone giyur (man)
A woman who has undergone giyur
The covenant of the Almighty with the people of Israel
questions.explanation: All four words are introduced in the lesson: ger and giyoret, ger tzedek and brit — the covenant that the ger enters.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is the Giyur Beit Din

questions.prompt: What is a non-Jew living in the Land of Israel and observing the seven laws of the descendants of Noah called?
questions.explanation: This is a “ger toshav” — unlike a “ger tzedek,” who has become Jewish through giyur.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is the Giyur Beit Din

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain: why is the decision about giyur made by the beit din and not by the candidate themselves?
questions.modelAnswer: I understand that giyur is not the signing of a paper and not an exam, but entering into the covenant that the Almighty made with the people of Israel at Mount Sinai. A covenant is not only my personal matter: by entering it I join a people, so the decision must be confirmed by judges. A beit din of three checks my sincerity and my acceptance of the mitzvot, and then performs the rites. This is close to my heart: I want to enter the people honestly and openly, before judges as witnesses.
keyPoints: Giyur is entering a covenant (brit), not a formality
The decision is a judicial act performed by the beit din
Openness and judges as witnesses
questions.explanation: The lesson says directly: the decision about giyur is made not by one person and not by the candidate themselves, but by the beit din — the Jewish court.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is the Giyur Beit Din

questions.prompt: Why is no offering brought today during giyur? What does this change for a man and for a woman?
questions.modelAnswer: The Rambam writes that the people entered the covenant through circumcision, immersion, and an offering. Today there is no Temple, so no offering is brought. A man undergoes circumcision and immersion, a woman — immersion. And one more thing: without kabbalat mitzvot, the acceptance of the mitzvot before the beit din, neither water nor circumcision by itself makes a person a Jew.
keyPoints: No offering is brought because there is no Temple
Man: circumcision and immersion; woman: immersion
Kabbalat mitzvot remains necessary
questions.explanation: The lesson reports the Rambam: an offering was part of the covenant, but without the Temple it is not brought. A man is left with circumcision and immersion, a woman with immersion. Kabbalat mitzvot is necessary in all this: without it the rites do not make a person a Jew.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 13:1–4

questions.prompt: At what moment, according to the Talmud, is the candidate told part of the mitzvot again?
questions.modelAnswer: According to Yevamot, part of the mitzvot is told again at the immersion: two sages do this. For a man, before tevilah come circumcision and healing. I will come to the mikveh ready to hear the mitzvot once more and to confirm that I accept them. For me this is part of the court procedure, not a random phrase by the water.
keyPoints: They are told again at the immersion
Two sages do this
For a man, immersion comes after circumcision and healing
questions.explanation: Yevamot 47b describes the procedure for the one who comes: circumcision, and after healing immersion, and at the immersion two sages tell part of the mitzvot again.
questions.source: Talmud, Yevamot 47a–b

questions.prompt: What is the name of the Conservative movement of Judaism in Israel and Europe?
options: Masorti
Karaism
Hasidism
Sephardic rite
questions.explanation: The lesson says: the Conservative movement in Israel and Europe is called Masorti.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: What does the candidate receive after completing giyur, in addition to a Jewish name?
options: Israeli citizenship
A yeshiva graduation diploma
A giyur certificate
A rabbi's certificate
questions.explanation: The common steps for all movements end with receiving a Jewish name and a document (certificate) of giyur.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: How does the Masorti approach to halacha differ from the Orthodox one?
options: Halacha is considered binding, but developing, and interpreted by the rabbis of the movement
Halacha is recognized as non-binding, and each person chooses the mitzvot independently
Halacha is replaced by the decisions of the community assembly
Halacha is observed only on festivals
questions.explanation: Conservative Judaism considers halacha binding but developing: it is interpreted by the rabbis of the movement (the Committee on Jewish Law of the Rabbinical Assembly).
questions.source: Masorti / Rabbinical Assembly (Derakhim)

questions.prompt: Who conducts state giyur in Israel?
options: Each local synagogue independently
The Jewish Agency (Sochnut)
The World Zionist Organization
Special courts attached to the Chief Rabbinate
questions.explanation: The lesson says: in Israel, state giyur is conducted by special courts attached to the Chief Rabbinate; preparatory programs also exist (for example, “Nativ”).
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: The Law of Return of 1950 gives every Jew the right to make aliyah to Israel.
questions.explanation: This is what the lesson says: the Law of Return (1950) gives every Jew the right to make aliyah to Israel.
questions.source: Law of Return (Israel, 1950; amendment 1970)

questions.prompt: The Chief Rabbinate of Israel recognizes all Orthodox batei din abroad without exception.
questions.explanation: The Chief Rabbinate recognizes not all Orthodox batei din abroad, but only those it has approved, so it is important to find out the status of the beit din in advance.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: Match each organization with its description.
pairs: Association of Progressive Judaism in Russia and the CIS countries
The World Union for Progressive Judaism
The Progressive movement that conducts giyur in Israel
The Conservative movement in Israel and Europe
questions.explanation: ROOPI and WUPJ are the Progressive movement, IMPJ is its Israeli branch, Masorti is the Conservative movement.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: What is the name of the preparatory program for giyur in Israel mentioned in the lesson?
questions.explanation: Among the Israeli preparatory programs, the lesson names “Nativ.”
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, in what do all the movements of Judaism agree with one another despite their differences?
questions.modelAnswer: I understand that all the movements agree on the main thing: giyur is a serious, well-considered decision that requires study, life in the community, and a beit din. In every movement the candidate declares that they are binding their fate to the people of Israel and its Torah. What differs is not the fact of the commitment, but what exactly is accepted as binding and who may be a judge. It matters to me that my choice of movement is a conscious decision, not an accident.
keyPoints: All movements require study, life in the community, and a beit din
Everywhere the candidate binds their fate to the people of Israel and its Torah
The difference lies in the understanding of the binding force of the mitzvot and in the composition of the beit din
questions.explanation: The lesson says directly: all the movements agree that giyur requires study, life in the community, and a beit din, and that the candidate binds their fate to the people of Israel.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: What do you need to find out in advance if it is important to you to be able to marry through the Israeli Rabbinate?
questions.modelAnswer: I know that religious recognition of giyur in Israel currently extends only to Orthodox giyur approved by the Rabbinate, and that the Chief Rabbinate recognizes not all batei din abroad. So I will find out in advance the status of the beit din I choose — whether it is approved by the Rabbinate. This is a question of my future and the future of my children, so I will not put it off. I will speak about it openly with my rabbi before beginning the path.
keyPoints: Religious recognition does not coincide with civil recognition
The Rabbinate recognizes only approved Orthodox giyur
The status of the beit din must be found out in advance
questions.explanation: The lesson says: if it matters to you to be able to marry through the Rabbinate, find out the status of the beit din you choose in advance.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

questions.prompt: How does the acceptance of the mitzvot in a Conservative beit din differ from an Orthodox one — and how should one speak about this honestly?
questions.modelAnswer: In an Orthodox beit din, the acceptance of the mitzvot is the readiness to observe halacha fully, including Shabbat without travel. In the Conservative movement halacha is also binding, but as interpreted by the rabbis of the movement: many communities allow driving to the synagogue on Shabbat, and men and women pray together. If I am asked, I will name the commitments of my own community and will not pass off someone else's custom as my own.
keyPoints: Orthodox giyur: full observance of halacha
Masorti: halacha is binding as interpreted by the rabbis of the movement
Examples from the lesson: driving to the synagogue on Shabbat and prayer together
Speak about the practice of your own community
questions.explanation: The lesson describes Conservative giyur in exactly this way: the candidate accepts Shabbat, kashrut, and the other mitzvot as Conservative halacha understands them.
questions.source: Lesson: The Path to Giyur in the Different Movements

differs.text: In Reform giyur, kabbalat mitzvot is not the acceptance of halacha as law in the Conservative or Orthodox sense, but knowledge, sincerity, and life in the community: the person consciously decides for themselves which mitzvot to observe and how.

questions.prompt: Which of these might you be asked to do at an interview with the beit din?
options: Read a short prayer in Hebrew
Write a commentary on the Talmud
Translate the entire Torah from memory
Give a lecture on Jewish history
questions.explanation: The section on knowledge says: sometimes they ask you to read a short prayer in Hebrew.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: What balance, according to the lesson, is important in an answer about non-Jewish parents?
options: Only firmness, without talking with the parents
Both respect for the parents and firmness about your decision
Only respect, even if it means giving up giyur
A complete break with the family for the sake of the fastest possible giyur
questions.explanation: The lesson says: a good answer shows both respect for the parents and firmness of decision.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: What details of practice might be checked in an Orthodox beit din?
options: The color of the candles for lighting and their price
Only the order of the blessings after a meal
Heating food on Shabbat, muktzeh, and checking eggs for blood spots
Table manners at the community table
questions.explanation: The Orthodox block lists: whether food may be heated on Shabbat, what muktzeh is, how eggs are checked for blood spots.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: How is one expected to dress for an interview at an Orthodox beit din?
options: In white, as on Yom Kippur, regardless of gender
In formal suits with ties
Whatever is comfortable; the main thing is clean clothes
Modestly: men in a kippah, women in a skirt with shoulders covered; married women with their heads covered
questions.explanation: The lesson's list of advice: dress modestly and neatly; to an Orthodox beit din men come in a kippah, women in a skirt with shoulders covered, married women with covered heads.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: At the interview it is more convincing to talk about what “Jews must do,” not about your own practice.
questions.explanation: The lesson advises speaking about yourself: “I do,” “I feel,” rather than “Jews must.”
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: In an Orthodox beit din it is enough to honestly say that you do not accept the coming of Mashiach as true: doubt replaces this assent.
questions.explanation: Doubts are a normal part of the life of a believer, but here the acceptance of the fundamentals as truth is obligatory: the whole Torah, including the Oral Torah, reward and punishment, and the coming of Mashiach. This rests on the Rambam's thirteen principles.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: Match each interview situation with the right course of action.
pairs: Admit it honestly rather than inventing things
Don't be afraid of a pause
questions.explanation: This advice is collected in the lesson: ask again if something is unclear; don't invent things; don't be afraid of a pause; speak about yourself.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: Which prayer is usually checked at the interview, along with its meaning?
questions.explanation: In the section on knowledge, the first thing named as checked is the Shema and its meaning.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: What three things does the beit din want to see in a candidate, and how will you show each one?
questions.modelAnswer: The judges want to see that the decision is sincere, that I understand what I am committing to, and that I am already living a Jewish life in the measure my community expects. I will show the first with my own story, not a generic text. The second — with my own words about Shabbat, kashrut, and prayer. The third — with an account of how my week actually goes. Knowledge matters, but these three things are checked before lists.
keyPoints: Sincerity of the decision
Understanding of the commitments
A Jewish life already begun, in the measure the community expects
questions.explanation: From the very beginning the lesson names these three things: sincerity, understanding of the commitments, and the life the candidate already leads.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: How will you answer questions about Jewish knowledge: what is usually checked, and what should you do if you have forgotten a fact?
questions.modelAnswer: I know that the basics are usually checked: the Shema and its meaning, the blessings over food, the order of the festivals, the meaning of Yom Kippur and Pesach, the basic laws of Shabbat and kashrut, why we eat matzah, who the Patriarchs and Matriarchs are. I am ready to read a short prayer in Hebrew. If I forget some fact, I will say so calmly: the lesson teaches that there is no need to worry about a single forgotten fact. What matters is that I have studied seriously and understand the meaning, not that I cram by rote.
keyPoints: The list of the basics checked, from the lesson
The possibility of reading a prayer in Hebrew
A calm attitude toward forgotten facts
questions.explanation: The section on knowledge lists what is checked and reassures: don't worry about a single forgotten fact.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview: Typical Questions and How to Answer Them

questions.prompt: What does the word “mikveh” mean in translation?
options: “A gathering of waters”
“Sacred fire”
“House of prayer”
“Mountain of blessing”
questions.explanation: Mikveh means “a gathering (of waters)”: a pool of natural water with a volume of no less than 40 seah.
questions.source: Vayikra 11:36

questions.prompt: For what else, besides giyur, is the mikveh used?
options: Babies are bathed in it before brit milah
Women immerse according to the laws of family purity, and new dishes are dipped
Hands are washed in it before every prayer
Wine for kiddush is prepared in it
questions.explanation: The lesson lists: married women immerse according to the laws of family purity, many men do so before Shabbat and Yom Kippur, and new dishes are dipped in a dish mikveh.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

questions.prompt: How is the presence of natural water arranged in modern mikvaot?
options: Natural water can be replaced by any water if the pool is deep
Only tap water, carefully sanctified
A reservoir of rainwater is connected to the pool in a special way
Natural water is added only once a year, on Yom Kippur
questions.explanation: Modern mikvaot usually have a reservoir of rainwater connected to the pool in a special way, while the water in the pool may be heated and purified.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

questions.prompt: What is the minimum volume of a kosher mikveh?
options: 10 seah — about two buckets
100 seah — an entire Olympic swimming pool
2 seah — a few mugs
40 seah — by various calculations, several hundred liters
questions.explanation: The minimum volume of a mikveh is 40 seah — by various calculations, several hundred liters — enough for an adult to immerse completely.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

differs.text: The volume of 40 seah is the measure of a kosher mikveh in halacha, as the lesson gives it. In Reform Judaism, tevilah is understood as a spiritual symbol of transition; in ROOPI communities and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it. The immersion is sometimes performed in a natural body of water, and prayers and the candidate's own words are added to it.

questions.prompt: The sea, a natural lake, or a river can never serve as a mikveh.
questions.explanation: According to halacha, the sea, a natural lake, or a river can also serve as a mikveh, but with qualifications, so the decision to immerse in a natural body of water is made by a rabbi.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

questions.prompt: If during immersion a strand of hair remains above the water, the immersion still counts once the hair is wet.
questions.explanation: If even a strand of hair remains above the water, the immersion is repeated: the water must cover the whole body and all the hair at the same time.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 198; 268:2–3

questions.prompt: Match each detail of tevilah with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: A custom right after the blessing “al ha-tevilah”
This is done in many communities
Does not replace a kosher mikveh for a person's tevilah
questions.explanation: After the blessing, by custom one immerses again, and in many communities a third time as well. Dipping new dishes is a separate mikveh: for giyur a mikveh for people is required.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

questions.prompt: What is the name of the pool of natural water in which the immersion is performed?
questions.explanation: Mikveh means “a gathering of waters,” a pool of natural water used for purification and for giyur.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

questions.prompt: You have come out of the mikveh. What words do many say first, and what does the beit din do with the document and the name?
questions.modelAnswer: Coming out of the water, I am already a Jew. Many at this moment say “Shema Yisrael” — the first declaration of faith already inside the people. Then the beit din presents the giyur certificate and, as a rule, announces the new Jewish name. I want to meet this calmly: the Shema here is not an additional exam, but the first words of a Jew.
keyPoints: Many say “Shema Yisrael” right after tevilah
The beit din presents the giyur certificate
As a rule, the new name is announced at the same time
questions.explanation: The lesson ends the order of tevilah this way: many gerim say “Shema Yisrael,” then the beit din presents the document and usually announces the name.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, tevilah is understood as a spiritual symbol of transition; in the communities of ROOPI (the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities) and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it. The immersion is sometimes performed in a natural body of water, with prayers and the candidate's own words added.

questions.prompt: According to Orthodox practice, how is the body positioned during immersion, and what does the word “kosher” mean?
questions.modelAnswer: The body must be relaxed: the arms slightly away from the body, the eyes and lips closed, but without clenching tightly, so that the water touches the outer folds. I do not press my arms to myself or clench. The balanit or the attendant watches the immersion and, after a valid immersion, says “kosher.” I wait for this word calmly: it confirms that the water covered the body as it should.
keyPoints: The body is relaxed, the arms slightly away
The eyes and lips are closed without tight clenching
“Kosher” is said by the balanit or the attendant after a valid immersion
questions.explanation: This is how the lesson describes the Orthodox practice of immersion and the word with which the attendant marks a valid tevilah.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

questions.prompt: You are offered to do tevilah in a river near home, without asking a rabbi. What will you do?
questions.modelAnswer: I will not choose the place on my own. According to halacha, the sea, a lake, or a river can serve as a mikveh, but with qualifications — the lesson mentions rivers fed by rain in particular. So it is the rabbi who permits a natural body of water, not the convenience of the day. I will ask him, and until his answer I will not immerse. If he says the river will not do, I will go to a mikveh where the natural water arrived by itself.
keyPoints: The sea, a lake, or a river can serve as a mikveh only with qualifications
The decision about a natural body of water is made by the rabbi
Without his decision one does not immerse in a river
questions.explanation: The lesson permits the sea, a lake, and a river as a mikveh only with qualifications and directly gives the decision to the rabbi.
questions.source: Lesson: The Mikveh: The Ger's Immersion

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, tevilah is understood as a spiritual symbol of transition; in the communities of ROOPI (the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities) and in Israel it is part of giyur, while in North America some rabbis do not require it. The immersion is sometimes performed in a natural body of water, with prayers and the candidate's own words added.

questions.prompt: Who, according to the lesson, literally repeats the path of the Patriarch by undergoing brit milah?
options: An adult ger
A Jewish infant
A kohen before serving in the Temple
A bridegroom before the chuppah
questions.explanation: The lesson says: an adult ger undergoing brit milah literally repeats the path of the Patriarch Avraham, who was circumcised at the age of 99.

questions.prompt: Whom does tradition call the “father of gerim”?
options: Moshe
Avraham
Aharon
David
questions.explanation: Tradition sees Avraham as the “father of gerim”: he left his father's house and his former faith and followed the One G-d.

questions.prompt: Why is a male ger's tevilah usually performed only several weeks after his brit milah?
options: Because the beit din is busy with other matters
Because the mikveh is opened only once a month
Because after the circumcision time is needed for healing
Because first one has to learn all the blessings
questions.explanation: The lesson says: then time is needed for healing — usually several weeks; only after that does the tevilah take place (Yevamot 47b).
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46a–47b

questions.prompt: How does the timing of a ger's milah differ from that of a Jewish infant?
options: A ger's milah is performed on the eighth day and overrides Shabbat
A ger's milah is not performed on Shabbat and festivals, while an infant is circumcised on the eighth day even on Shabbat
A ger's milah is performed only in Jerusalem
An infant's milah is performed without a blessing
questions.explanation: An infant's milah on the eighth day overrides the prohibition of Shabbat. A ger's milah does not override this prohibition and is not performed on Shabbat and festivals.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1–5

differs.text: In the Reform movement of North America, brit milah for an adult ger is formally not obligatory. However, in ROOPI (the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities), according to the description of the giyur school “Shaarei Shalom,” brit milah for men is obligatory, as it is in Progressive giyur in Israel.

questions.prompt: A brit milah for an adult ger is performed by a mohel — a specialist who knows the laws of milah, often a physician — under local anesthesia.
questions.explanation: The lesson describes: the circumcision is performed by a mohel; for adults this is often a physician-mohel, the operation is performed in a clinic or a specially equipped room, under local anesthesia.
questions.source: Lesson: Brit milah, hatafat dam brit, and the new name

questions.prompt: Hatafat dam brit is a full second circumcision of an already circumcised man.
questions.explanation: Hatafat dam brit is only the symbolic extraction of a drop of the covenant's blood: a tiny prick that takes a minute and is almost painless.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 135a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 268:1

questions.prompt: Match the concept related to a ger's name with its description.
pairs: The patronymic of a male ger
A variant of the patronymic that includes the matriarch's name
The marriage contract in which a ger's name is written
An expression for the end of life: that is when the name is written on the tombstone
questions.explanation: A ger's name is “ben/bat Avraham Avinu” (in many communities, with Sarah). It is used when he is called up to the Torah, in the ketubah, and, after death, on the tombstone. “One hundred and twenty years” is an expression about the end of life, not the age at which the name starts being written.
questions.source: Rambam, Letter to Ovadyah the Ger; the custom of bestowing a ger's name

questions.prompt: What is the “covenant of circumcision” called in Hebrew?
questions.explanation: Brit milah — the “covenant of circumcision,” the sign of the Almighty's covenant with Avraham and his descendants.

questions.prompt: Why is a ger's brit milah not an ordinary medical operation? What must be correct in the rite itself?
questions.modelAnswer: For me this is a sign of the covenant, not a standalone operation. The circumcision must be performed specifically for the sake of the giyur, as an entry into the covenant. It is done by a mohel, and representatives of the beit din are present — according to many opinions, three judges. I will ask them in advance how the rite will proceed, and I do not schedule it myself as an ordinary medical procedure.
keyPoints: The milah is performed for the sake of the giyur, as an entry into the covenant
Representatives of the beit din are present (according to many opinions — three)
It is a rite of the covenant, not a standalone medical procedure
questions.explanation: The lesson requires that a ger's milah be part of entering the covenant and take place before representatives of the beit din, not as a mere medical procedure.
questions.source: Lesson: Brit milah, hatafat dam brit, and the new name

differs.text: In the Reform movement of North America, brit milah for an adult ger is formally not obligatory. However, in ROOPI (the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities), according to the description of the giyur school “Shaarei Shalom,” brit milah for men is obligatory, as it is in Progressive giyur in Israel.

questions.prompt: Why does a ger bear the patronymic “son (daughter) of Avraham” rather than that of his non-Jewish parents?
questions.modelAnswer: I understand: a Jewish name consists of a personal name and the father's name, but a ger's parents are not Jewish, so he is called a son of Avraham, our forefather. This expresses the main idea: I am not a “stranger” but a true son of Avraham and Sarah. Rambam wrote to Ovadyah the ger that a ger may say in prayer “our G-d and the G-d of our fathers,” because Avraham is his father. In many communities the foremother is added as well: “ben Avraham ve-Sarah.”
keyPoints: A ger's parents are not Jewish, so the patronymic follows Avraham
A ger is a true son of Avraham and Sarah
Rambam: “The G-d of our fathers” applies to a ger as well
questions.explanation: The lesson explains how a ger's Jewish name is constructed and what it means, citing Rambam's letter to Ovadyah the Ger.
questions.source: Rambam, Letter to Ovadyah the Ger

questions.prompt: How many times does the Torah warn against hurting a ger, according to the Talmud?
options: 7 times
18 times
36 times, according to another opinion — 46
613 times
questions.explanation: Bava Metzia 59b counts this warning 36 times, and according to another opinion — 46. The lesson says that no other mitzvah is repeated so often.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b

questions.prompt: According to Rambam, loving a ger comprises how many mitzvot?
options: One
Two
Three
Seven
questions.explanation: Rambam (Deot 6:4) explains: loving a ger is two mitzvot — “love your fellow” and the separate mitzvah of loving a ger.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Character Traits (De'ot) 6:4

questions.prompt: According to the Mishnah (Bava Metzia 4:10), what must one not say to a person who has repented of their past?
options: “Your people shall be my people”
“Go and learn”
“Remember your former deeds”
“Make for yourself a teacher”
questions.explanation: The Mishnah counts reminding someone of the past as ona'at devarim: one must not say to a penitent “remember your former deeds.”
questions.source: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10; Bava Metzia 58b–59b

questions.prompt: What marriage restriction applies to a giyoret under Orthodox halacha?
options: She cannot marry a Levite
She cannot marry before the age of 20
She cannot marry another ger
She cannot marry a kohen
questions.explanation: In Orthodox halacha, a giyoret cannot marry a kohen (Yevamot 60b; Rambam, Issurei Biah 18:3).
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 18:3

questions.prompt: A ger has the same communal rights as a Jew by birth: he is called up to the Torah, he counts in a minyan, and he can become a rabbi or the head of a congregation.
questions.explanation: The lesson lists precisely these rights: being called up to the Torah, the minyan, and the possibility of becoming a rabbi, a scholar, and the head of a congregation.
questions.source: Lesson: After the Giyur — the Life of a Ger

questions.prompt: The Book of Ruth is read on Shavuot — the festival of the giving of the Torah.
questions.explanation: The lesson begins with the fact that the Book of Ruth is read on Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah.

questions.prompt: What is “hurting with words” called, including reminding a ger of their past or origin?
questions.explanation: Ona'at devarim is the prohibition against causing pain with words, including through reminders of the past or of non-Jewish origin.
questions.source: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10; Bava Metzia 58b–59b

questions.prompt: What does the comparison of a ger to a newborn baby mean?
questions.modelAnswer: I understand these words of the Talmud this way: my past sins no longer weigh upon me, and I am beginning a new life among the people of Israel. I am obligated to keep all the mitzvot, like any Jew, and I have all the rights: I will be called up to the Torah, I will count in a minyan. For me this is deeply personal: the giyur became my rebirth, and I want to live this new life worthily.
keyPoints: The past no longer weighs: a new life
Full obligations and rights, like any Jew
Yevamot 22a
questions.explanation: The Talmud (Yevamot 22a) says: a ger who has embraced Judaism is like a newborn baby — he begins a new life.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 22a, 47b

questions.prompt: What will you do if someone in the congregation tactlessly asks who you were before your giyur?
questions.modelAnswer: I know that reminding a ger of his past is ona'at devarim, hurtful words, and that I am not obligated to share my story.
