So I will gently say that this is personal — and that is my rightful prerogative. If I ever want to tell about my journey, I will do so myself, in my own time: gers' stories often inspire others. But I will not feel obliged to answer to anyone.
keyPoints: Reminding someone of the past is ona'at devarim
The right not to share one's story belongs to the ger
Telling one's story happens only by one's own free will
questions.explanation: The lesson says directly: you are entitled to gently say that this is personal; whether to share your story is a decision only you can make.
questions.source: Lesson: After the Giyur — the Life of a Ger

questions.prompt: If a giyoret gives birth to a child after her giyur, what will be the status of that child?
questions.modelAnswer: A child whom a giyoret gave birth to after her giyur is a Jew from birth and does not need a separate giyur. This is what the lesson says specifically about children born after the mother's immersion: at the time of the birth she is Jewish. I will raise such a child among the people of Israel and will not extend this rule to other cases on my own — I will ask a rabbi about my own family.
keyPoints: A child born to a giyoret after her giyur is a Jew from birth
Such a child does not need a separate giyur
The rule concerns a birth after the mother's giyur
questions.explanation: The lesson says: children born after the giyur — and for a giyoret these are the children she herself gives birth to — are Jews from birth.
questions.source: Lesson: After the Giyur — the Life of a Ger

questions.prompt: “Has Mashiach already come? What exactly does Judaism await?”
questions.modelAnswer: In Judaism, Mashiach has not yet come, and I await his coming, as Rambam's twelfth principle says: “though he tarries, I await him every day.” Mashiach is a human being, a king from the descendants of David — not G-d. According to Rambam, he will be recognized by his deeds: he will bring the people back to the Torah, rebuild the Temple, and gather the exiles (Laws of Kings 11:4). None of this has happened yet, so his coming will be the first and only one; the concept of a “second coming” does not exist in Judaism. We do not know when he will come, and there is no need to calculate the date — what is needed is to live by the Torah starting now.
keyPoints: Mashiach has not yet come; he is awaited
A human being, a king from the house of David — not G-d
Rambam's signs: Torah, the Temple, the exiles
His coming will be the first and only one: there is no “second coming”
The date is unknown; it is not to be calculated
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands the Jewish expectation of Mashiach and does not confuse it with the beliefs of other religions.
questions.source: Rambam, 13 Principles (12th); Laws of Kings 11:1–4; Sanhedrin 97b

questions.prompt: “Can G-d exist in three persons or appear in human form?”
questions.modelAnswer: No. I believe that G-d is one and indivisible: “Hear, O Israel: the L-rd is our G-d, the L-rd is one” (Devarim 6:4). His unity is unlike any other: He cannot be divided into parts or “persons,” and He has no body or form (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7–8). The Torah says: “G-d is not a man” (Bamidbar 23:19), therefore He does not become a human being, and no human being — not even Mashiach — is G-d. I pray only to the Almighty, without intermediaries. Teachings about G-d in three persons or about G-d becoming a human being are not Judaism; I respect my loved ones of another faith, but I do not share that faith.
keyPoints: G-d is one and indivisible (Shema, Devarim 6:4)
No body, no form, no “persons” (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7–8)
“G-d is not a man” (Bamidbar 23:19); Mashiach is not G-d
Prayer only to the Almighty; respect for loved ones without joining another faith
questions.explanation: Rambam requires explaining to the candidate in detail the unity of the Almighty and the prohibition of idolatry; this question checks that you have accepted this.
questions.source: Devarim 6:4; Bamidbar 23:19; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7–8; Laws of Forbidden Relations 14:2

questions.prompt: Describe how the Reform (Progressive) giyur works in the country and congregation where you are going to the beit din. How does this path differ from nineteenth-century North American practice, and what is already your practice?
questions.modelAnswer: I am going through a Progressive congregation and will first state its rules, not someone else's. In ROOPI, according to the “Shaarei Shalom” school's description, one needs a motivation letter, at least a year of study, regular life in the community, a beit din and mikveh, and for men brit milah is mandatory. In Israel the giyur is conducted by IMPJ, and after the Supreme Court's 2021 decision it is recognized for civil status, but not by the Chief Rabbinate. In North America the CCAR's 1892 resolution formally did not make mikveh and milah mandatory, yet today many rabbis require or strongly recommend them, while the year of study and community life remain the framework. I am already studying, attending services, and ready for the rituals my congregation requires.
keyPoints: State the rules of your own congregation, not of another country
ROOPI: a motivation letter, a year of study, community life, beit din, mikveh, brit milah for men
Israel: IMPJ, civil recognition by the 2021 decision, without recognition by the Rabbinate
North America: the 1892 resolution and a more ritually observant practice today
questions.explanation: The judges want to hear your actual path, not the general phrase “in Reform it is easier.”
questions.source: “Shaarei Shalom” giyur school; CCAR 1892; IMPJ; Supreme Court of Israel, 2021

questions.prompt: What is informed choice of mitzvot in Reform Judaism? Give examples from your own life and explain how it differs both from arbitrariness and from accepting all of halacha as a binding code.
questions.modelAnswer: Informed choice means: I first study what the tradition says, how the generations lived this mitzvah, and how my congregation understands it, and only then do I decide how to fulfill it in my own life. It is not “anything goes for me” and not a rejection of study. For me, for example, Shabbat means candles, kiddush, services, and abstaining from work and shopping, and kashrut means abstaining from the animals forbidden by the Torah and separating meat and dairy at home. I do not accept the 39 melachot as a legal code, but neither do I call ignorance a choice. The covenant, for me, is a living responsibility that I carry honestly and intend to deepen after my giyur.
keyPoints: First study and the congregation's voice, then a personal decision
It is not arbitrariness and not “in Reform you can observe nothing”
Concrete examples of a practice already being lived
Readiness to keep growing after the giyur
questions.explanation: This is one of the most characteristic questions of a Progressive beit din.
questions.source: Lesson “Reform Giyur: Study, Community, and Beit Din”; CCAR materials

questions.prompt: How is a Reform giyur recognized within different Jewish frameworks: in Progressive congregations, in Conservative ones, under the Law of Return, and by the Chief Rabbinate of Israel? Why should a candidate know this difference before beginning the journey?
questions.modelAnswer: A Reform giyur is recognized by Progressive congregations and by many Conservative ones, especially if there was study, a beit din, mikveh, and brit milah. The State of Israel recognizes it for the Law of Return: both a giyur performed abroad and, after the Supreme Court's 2021 decision, a Progressive giyur performed inside the country — for civil status. The Chief Rabbinate of Israel and Orthodox batei din do not recognize it, including for marriage through the Rabbinate. This is not a judgment of a person's worth, but the different rules of different institutions. You need to know them in advance if you are thinking about moving, about marriage, and about which congregation your children will live in — and still choose the path in which you want to live.
keyPoints: Recognition by Progressive and many Conservative congregations
The Law of Return and the 2021 decision — civil status
The Rabbinate and Orthodox courts do not recognize it
Know it in advance, without self-deception, and still choose your own path
questions.explanation: An honest conversation about recognition is part of entering the people as an adult.
questions.source: The Law of Return; Supreme Court of Israel, 2021; the lesson on Reform giyur

questions.prompt: What exactly did the Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR) resolve in 1892 regarding the rituals of giyur?
options: Brit milah and tevilah are not formally mandatory; the procedure is determined by the rabbi and the congregation
Brit milah and tevilah have been mandatory in all Reform congregations of the world since then
A Reform giyur can proceed without study if there is a Jewish spouse
Giyur is permitted only in the Land of Israel and only through the Chief Rabbinate
questions.explanation: The 1892 resolution left milah and mikveh to the rabbi's discretion; today's practice in many congregations is more ritually observant.
questions.source: CCAR Resolution of 1892

questions.prompt: According to the “Shaarei Shalom” congregation's giyur school description, which of the following is part of ROOPI Progressive giyur?
options: A motivation letter, at least a year of study, life in the community, a beit din, mikveh; for men brit milah is mandatory
Only an interview with one rabbi and a declaration of faith without study
Two years of living in an Orthodox neighborhood and giving up secular work
Only immersion in a natural body of water without a beit din
questions.explanation: In ROOPI the path is complete in its rituals: study, community, court, mikveh, and brit milah for men.
questions.source: “Shaarei Shalom” Giyur School (ROOPI)

questions.prompt: What did the Supreme Court of Israel's 2021 decision change for a Progressive giyur performed inside the country?
options: It is recognized for civil status and the Law of Return, but not by the Chief Rabbinate
It has since fully replaced Orthodox giyur for marriage through the Rabbinate
It was banned on the territory of Israel
It is recognized only if the candidate is already serving in the army
questions.explanation: The 2021 decision concerns civil recognition, not religious status with the Rabbinate.
questions.source: Supreme Court of Israel, 2021

questions.prompt: How does the CCAR's 1983 resolution define the Jewishness of a child?
options: The child of one Jewish parent — a mother or a father — is Jewish if they are raised as a Jew
Jewishness is transmitted only through the father, as in some ancient peoples
Jewishness is transmitted only through the mother, and the movement knows no exceptions
A child is considered Jewish automatically, even if they are not raised in Judaism
questions.explanation: This decision applies within the Reform movement; Orthodox and Conservative Judaism proceed from the maternal line.
questions.source: CCAR Resolution of 1983

questions.prompt: Informed choice in Reform Judaism means that mitzvot may be left unstudied if they are inconvenient for you.
questions.explanation: First study and the voice of tradition, and only then an honest personal decision. Ignorance is not a choice.
questions.source: Lesson on Reform giyur; CCAR materials

questions.prompt: Reform giyur is a lightened copy of the Orthodox one: less study and less seriousness, but the very same obligations.
questions.explanation: It is a different path within the people, with its own depth: study, community, beit din, and an honest covenant — not “lightened Orthodoxy.”
questions.source: Lesson “Reform Giyur: Study, Community, and Beit Din”

questions.prompt: The Chief Rabbinate of Israel marries couples on the basis of a Progressive giyur performed in Israel after 2021.
questions.explanation: The 2021 decision concerns civil status. Religious marriage through the Rabbinate still requires an Orthodox giyur.
questions.source: Supreme Court of Israel, 2021; practice of the Chief Rabbinate

questions.prompt: What is the name of the principle in Reform Judaism by which a mitzvah is first studied and then consciously taken into one's life? (two words, or the English term)
questions.explanation: The usual Russian term is “osoznanny vybor”; in the movement's English-language documents — “informed choice.”
questions.source: CCAR / URJ materials

questions.prompt: What is the Israeli Progressive movement that conducts Reform giyur in Israel called? (abbreviation)
questions.explanation: IMPJ — the Israeli branch of Progressive Judaism.
questions.source: https://giyur.reform.org.il/ru/

questions.prompt: Match the framework of recognition with its typical attitude toward Reform giyur.
pairs: They recognize their own movement's giyur
Civil status, including giyur in Israel
Does not recognize it for religious marriage
They often recognize it if there was study, a court, and rituals
questions.explanation: It is important to distinguish recognition by a congregation, by civil law, and by the Rabbinate.
questions.source: Lesson on Reform giyur

questions.prompt: Who usually makes up a Reform giyur beit din?
options: Three rabbis of the Progressive movement
Nine judges of the Chief Rabbinate
One congregation elder without rabbinic ordination
Twelve witnesses who themselves went through giyur
questions.explanation: As in other movements, the giyur court usually consists of three; here these are rabbis of the Progressive movement.
questions.source: Practice of the CCAR / WUPJ / ROOPI

questions.prompt: Which answer is considered weak at a Reform beit din when the conversation turns to mitzvot?
options: “In Reform it is not obligatory, so I observe nothing”
“I have studied the tradition; this is what I already keep, and this is what I am moving toward”
“For me Shabbat is candles, services, and abstaining from weekday work”
“I have taken on kashrut to the extent I can honestly keep”
questions.explanation: Appealing to “non-obligatoriness” without study and practice is a rejection of informed choice, not its application.
questions.source: Lesson on Reform giyur

questions.prompt: What is worth checking when choosing a congregation before giyur?
options: Only the convenience of the schedule
Which movement it belongs to, who the rabbi is, and what they teach about G-d, Mashiach, and the Torah
Only whether there is a kippah and kiddush there
Whether there are enough free holiday meals
questions.explanation: External appearances do not replace checking the teaching and affiliation with a known movement.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview; the lesson on how to read the Tanakh

questions.prompt: If at the beit din you are asked about your former faith, it is enough to say that you now believe in the one G-d, pray only to Him, and do not take part in other religious services.
questions.explanation: The judges expect clarity and calm, not polemics and not memorized railing.
questions.source: Lesson: The Interview; Rambam, Principles 1–5 and 12

questions.prompt: How should a ger treat an invitation to a gathering that looks Jewish but teaches that Mashiach has already come?
options: Go along, since the kippah and tallit already prove everything
Politely decline and discuss it with your rabbi
Argue there alone until you "win"
Decide that after giyur such meetings no longer matter
questions.explanation: Loyalty to the covenant means not arguing alone and not entering a congregation with a different teaching just because of its outward "Jewishness".
questions.source: Lesson: After Giyur; CCAR, 1985

questions.prompt: For a ger, accepting after giyur a teaching that the Torah has been replaced, or that the Mashiach has already come, means calling the very meaning of his giyur into question.
questions.explanation: Giyur is an entry into the covenant forever. Loyalty to G-d, to the Torah, and to the people is the heart of this step.
questions.source: Lesson: After Giyur

questions.prompt: According to Rambam, the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the World to Come. Then why do we need giyur?
options: Without giyur no one can have a share in the World to Come
Giyur is not a "ticket to the future" but an entry into the covenant of the people of Israel, into the Torah and the mitzvot
Giyur is only needed for the paperwork
Giyur replaces repentance for the nations of the world
questions.explanation: A righteous non-Jew already has a share (Rambam, Laws of Kings 8:11). Giyur is joining the people and the full covenant.
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Kings 8:11; Yevamot 47a

questions.prompt: The judge asks: "What will you answer if someone tells you that G-d became a human being, or that the Mashiach has already come?"
questions.modelAnswer: I will answer calmly: in Judaism G-d is one, indivisible, without body or form, and I pray only to Him. The teaching of a G-d who became human, or of a G-d in several persons, is not Judaism. The Mashiach is a human being from the house of David, and he will be recognized by what is accomplished in this world: the Temple, the ingathering of the exiles, peace, the Torah. As long as this has not happened, he has not yet come, and we do not await any "second coming." I will not argue alone: if the conversation goes further, I will go to my rabbi.
keyPoints: G-d is one, without body or "persons"
The Mashiach has not yet come; the criteria are unfulfilled
That is not Judaism — said without hostility
When in doubt — go to a rabbi, don't argue alone
questions.explanation: A typical beit din question for those who grew up in a different environment. What matters is clarity and respect, not polemical eagerness.
questions.source: Rambam, principles 1–5, 12; Laws of Kings 11:4
